entries.d80c626e6d777d885032a7e4666b788ac70833cf: <div sID="gen26960" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="John.5" sID="John.5"/> <div eID="gen26960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26961" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26962" type="x-p"/> We have in the gospels a faithful record of all that Jesus began both to do and to teach, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.1">Acts i. 1</reference>. These two are interwoven, because what he taught explained what he did, and what he did confirmed what he taught. Accordingly, we have in this chapter a miracle and a sermon. I. The miracle was the cure of an impotent man that had been diseased thirty-eight years, with the circumstances of that cure, <reference osisRef="John.5.1-John.5.16">ver. 1-16</reference>. II. The sermon was Christ's vindication of himself before the sanhedrim, when he was prosecuted as a criminal for healing the man on the sabbath day, in which, 1. He asserts his authority as Messiah, and Mediator between God and man, <reference osisRef="John.5.17-John.5.29">ver. 17-29</reference>. 2. He proves it by the testimony of his Father, of John Baptist, of his miracles, and of the scriptures of the Old Testament, and condemns the Jews for their unbelief, <reference osisRef="John.5.30-John.5.47">ver. 30-47</reference>.
entries.14f1cf4ffa9a40e5c270f9e08f3cc969bb84004a: <div eID="gen26962" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26961" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cure at the Pool of Bethesda.</title> <div sID="gen26963" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After this there was a feast of the Jews; and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep <hi type="italic">market</hi> a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches. <hi type="super">3</hi> In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water. <hi type="super">4</hi> For an angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water: whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in was made whole of whatsoever disease he had. <hi type="super">5</hi> And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years. <hi type="super">6</hi> When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time <hi type="italic">in that case,</hi> he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole? <hi type="super">7</hi> The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me. <hi type="super">8</hi> Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk. <hi type="super">9</hi> And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath. <hi type="super">10</hi> The Jews therefore said unto him that was cured, It is the sabbath day: it is not lawful for thee to carry <hi type="italic">thy</hi> bed. <hi type="super">11</hi> He answered them, He that made me whole, the same said unto me, Take up thy bed, and walk. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then asked they him, What man is that which said unto thee, Take up thy bed, and walk? <hi type="super">13</hi> And he that was healed wist not who it was: for Jesus had conveyed himself away, a multitude being in <hi type="italic">that</hi> place. <hi type="super">14</hi> Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole. <hi type="super">16</hi> And therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus, and sought to slay him, because he had done these things on the sabbath day. <div eID="gen26963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26964" type="x-p"/> This miraculous cure is not recorded by any other of the evangelists, who confine themselves mostly to the miracles wrought in Galilee, but John relates those wrought at Jerusalem. Concerning this observe, <div eID="gen26964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26965" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">The time when</hi> this cure was wrought: it was at a <hi type="italic">feast of the Jews,</hi> that is, the passover, for that was the most celebrated feast. Christ, though residing in Galilee, yet <hi type="italic">went up to Jerusalem</hi> at the feast, <reference osisRef="John.5.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. Because it was an <hi type="italic">ordinance of God,</hi> which, as a <hi type="italic">subject,</hi> he would observe, being made under the law; though as a <hi type="italic">Son</hi> he might have pleaded an exemption. Thus he would teach us to attend religious assemblies. <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">Heb. x. 25</reference>. 2. Because it was an <hi type="italic">opportunity of good;</hi> for, (1.) there were great numbers gathered together there at that time; it was a general rendezvous, at least of all serious thinking people, from all parts of the country, besides proselytes from other nations: and Wisdom must <hi type="italic">cry in the places of concourse,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 21</reference>. (2.) It was to be hoped that they were in a <hi type="italic">good frame,</hi> for they came together to <hi type="italic">worship God</hi> and to spend their time in religious exercises. Now a mind <hi type="italic">inclined to devotion,</hi> and sequestering itself to the exercises of piety, <hi type="italic">lies very open</hi> to the further discoveries of divine light and love, and to it Christ will be acceptable. <div eID="gen26965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26966" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">place where</hi> this cure was wrought: at the <hi type="italic">pool of Bethesda,</hi> which had a miraculous healing virtue in it, and is here particularly described, <reference osisRef="John.5.2-John.5.4">v. 2-4</reference>. <div eID="gen26966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26967" type="x-p"/> 1. Where it was situated: <hi type="italic">At Jerusalem, by the sheep-market;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epi te probatike</hi></hi>. It might as well be rendered the <hi type="italic">sheep-cote,</hi> where the sheep were kept, or the <hi type="italic">sheep-gate,</hi> which we read of, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Neh. iii. 1</reference>, through which the sheep were <hi type="italic">brought,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">sheep-market,</hi> where they were <hi type="italic">sold.</hi> Some think it was near the temple, and, if so, it yielded a melancholy but profitable spectacle to those that went up to the temple to pray. <div eID="gen26967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26968" type="x-p"/> 2. How it was called: It was a <hi type="italic">pool</hi> (a pond or bath), <hi type="italic">which is called in Hebrew, Bethesda—the house of mercy;</hi> for therein appeared much of the <hi type="italic">mercy of God</hi> to the sick and diseased. In a world of so much misery as this is, it is well that there are some <hi type="italic">Bethesdas—houses of mercy</hi> (remedies against those maladies), that the scene is not all melancholy. An <hi type="italic">alms-house,</hi> so Dr. Hammond. Dr. Lightfoot's conjecture is that this was the <hi type="italic">upper pool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Isa. vii. 3</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">old pool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa. xxii. 11</reference>; that it had been used for <hi type="italic">washing</hi> from ceremonial pollutions, for convenience of which the porches were built to dress and undress in, but it was lately become medicinal. <div eID="gen26968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26969" type="x-p"/> 3. How it was fitted up: It had <hi type="italic">five porches, cloisters, piazzas,</hi> or <hi type="italic">roofed walks,</hi> in which the sick lay. Thus the charity of men concurred with the mercy of God for the relief of the distressed. Nature has provided <hi type="italic">remedies,</hi> but men must provide <hi type="italic">hospitals.</hi> <div eID="gen26969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26970" type="x-p"/> 4. How it was frequented with sick and cripples (<reference osisRef="John.5.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">In these lay a great multitude of impotent folks.</hi> How many are the afflictions of the afflicted in this world! How full of complaints are all places, and what multitudes of impotent folks! It may do us good to visit the hospitals sometimes, that we may take occasion, from the calamities of others, to thank God for our comforts. The evangelist specifies three sorts of diseased people that lay here, <hi type="italic">blind, halt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">withered</hi> or <hi type="italic">sinew—shrunk,</hi> either in one particular part, as the man with the <hi type="italic">withered hand,</hi> or all over paralytic. These are mentioned because, being least able to help themselves into the water, they lay longest waiting in the <hi type="italic">porches.</hi> Those that were sick of these bodily diseases took the pains to come <hi type="italic">far</hi> and had the patience to wait <hi type="italic">long</hi> for a cure; any of us would have done the same, and we ought to do so: but O that men were as wise for their souls, and as solicitous to get their spiritual diseases healed! We are all by nature <hi type="italic">impotent folks</hi> in spiritual things, <hi type="italic">blind, halt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">withered;</hi> but effectual provision is made for our cure if we will but observe orders. <div eID="gen26970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26971" type="x-p"/> 5. What virtue it had for the cure of these impotent folks (<reference osisRef="John.5.4">v. 4</reference>). <hi type="italic">An angel went down,</hi> and <hi type="italic">troubled the water;</hi> and <hi type="italic">whoso first stepped in was made whole.</hi> That this strange virtue in the pool was <hi type="italic">natural,</hi> or <hi type="italic">artificial</hi> rather, and was the effect of the washing of the sacrifices, which impregnated the water with I know not what healing virtue even for <hi type="italic">blind</hi> people, and that the angel was a <hi type="italic">messenger,</hi> a common person, sent down to stir the water, is altogether groundless; there was a room in the temple on purpose to wash the sacrifices in. Expositors generally agree that the virtue this pool had was supernatural. It is true the Jewish writers, who are not sparing in recounting the praises of Jerusalem, do none of them make the least mention of this <hi type="italic">healing pool,</hi> of which silence in this matter perhaps this is the reason, that it was taken for a presage of the near approach of the Messiah, and therefore those who denied him to be come industriously concealed such an indication of his coming; so that this is all the account we have of it. Observe, <div eID="gen26971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">preparation</hi> of the medicine by an angel, who <hi type="italic">went down into the pool,</hi> and <hi type="italic">stirred the water.</hi> Angels are God's servants, and friends to mankind; and perhaps are more active in the removing of diseases (as evil angels in the inflicting of them) than we are aware of. Raphael, the apocryphal name of an angel, signifies <hi type="italic">medicina Dei—God's physic,</hi> or <hi type="italic">physician</hi> rather. See what mean offices the holy angels condescend to, for the good of men. If we would do the will of God as the angels do it, we must think nothing below us but sin. The <hi type="italic">troubling of the water</hi> was the signal given of the descent of the angel, as the <hi type="italic">going upon the tops of the mulberry trees</hi> was to David, and then they must <hi type="italic">bestir themselves.</hi> The waters of the sanctuary are then <hi type="italic">healing</hi> when they are put in <hi type="italic">motion.</hi> Ministers must <hi type="italic">stir up the gift</hi> that is in them. When they are cold and dull in their ministrations, the waters <hi type="italic">settle,</hi> and are not apt to <hi type="italic">heal.</hi> The angel descended, to <hi type="italic">stir the water,</hi> not daily, perhaps not frequently, but <hi type="italic">at a certain season;</hi> some think, at the three solemn feasts, to grace those solemnities; or, <hi type="italic">now and then,</hi> as Infinite Wisdom saw fit. God is a free agent in dispensing his favours. <div eID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">operation</hi> of the medicine: <hi type="italic">Whoever first stepped in was made whole.</hi> here is, [1.] miraculous extent of the virtue as to the <hi type="italic">diseases</hi> cured; what disease soever it was, this water cured it. Natural and artificial baths are as <hi type="italic">hurtful</hi> in some cases as they are useful in others, but this was a remedy for every malady, even for those that came from contrary causes. The power of miracles <hi type="italic">succeeds</hi> where the power of nature <hi type="italic">succumbs.</hi> [2.] A miraculous limitation of the virtue as to the <hi type="italic">persons</hi> cured: He that first stepped in had the benefit; that is, he or they that stepped in immediately were cured, not those that lingered and came in afterwards. This teaches us to observe and improve our opportunities, and to <hi type="italic">look about us,</hi> that we slip not a season which may never return. The angel <hi type="italic">stirred</hi> the waters, but left the diseased to themselves to <hi type="italic">get in.</hi> God has put virtue into the scriptures and ordinances, for he would have healed us; but, if we do not make a due improvement of them, it is our own fault, we <hi type="italic">would not be healed.</hi> <div eID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26974" type="x-p"/> Now this is all the account we have of this <hi type="italic">standing</hi> miracle; it is uncertain when it began and when it ceased. Some conjecture it began when Eliashib the high priest began the building of the wall about Jerusalem, and sanctified it with prayer; and that God testified his acceptance by putting this virtue into the adjoining pool. Some think it began now lately at Christ's birth; nay, others at his baptism. Dr. Lightfoot, finding in <hi type="italic">Josephus, Antiq.</hi> 15. 121-122, mention of a great earthquake in the seventh year of Herod, thirty years before Christ's birth, supposed, since there used to be earthquakes at the descent of angels, that then the angel first descended to stir this water. Some think it ceased with this miracle, others at Christ's death; however, it is certain it had a gracious signification. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> it was a <hi type="italic">token</hi> of God's good will to that people, and an indication that, though they had been long without prophets and miracles, yet God had not <hi type="italic">cast them off;</hi> though they were now an oppressed despised people, and many were ready to say, <hi type="italic">Where are all the wonders that our fathers told us of?</hi> God did hereby let them know that he had still a kindness for the <hi type="italic">city of their solemnities.</hi> We may hence take occasion to acknowledge with thankfulness God's power and goodness in the mineral waters, that contribute so much to the health of mankind; for God <hi type="italic">made the fountains of water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was a type of the Messiah, who is the <hi type="italic">fountain opened;</hi> and was intended to raise people's expectations of him who is the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness,</hi> that arises <hi type="italic">with healing under his wings.</hi> These waters had formerly been used for purifying, now for healing, to signify both the <hi type="italic">cleansing</hi> and <hi type="italic">curing</hi> virtue of the blood of Christ, that incomparable bath, which <hi type="italic">heals all our diseases.</hi> The waters of Siloam, which filled this pool, signified the kingdom of David, and of Christ the Son of David (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa. viii. 6</reference>); fitly therefore have they now this <hi type="italic">sovereign</hi> virtue put into them. The laver of regeneration is to us as Bethesda's pool, healing our spiritual diseases; not at certain seasons, but at all times. <hi type="italic">Whoever will, let him come.</hi> <div eID="gen26974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> III. The patient on whom this cure was wrought (<reference osisRef="John.5.5">v. 5</reference>): one that <hi type="italic">had been infirm thirty-eight years.</hi> 1. His <hi type="italic">disease</hi> was <hi type="italic">grievous:</hi> He had an <hi type="italic">infirmity,</hi> a weakness; he had lost the use of his limbs, at least on one side, as is usual in palsies. It is sad to have the body so disabled that, instead of being the soul's instrument, it is become, even in the affairs of this life, its burden. What reason have we to thank God for bodily strength, to use it for him, and to pity those who are <hi type="italic">his prisoners!</hi> 2. The duration of it was <hi type="italic">tedious: Thirty-eight years.</hi> He was lame longer than most live. Many are so long disabled for the offices of life that, as the psalmist complains, they seem to be <hi type="italic">made in vain;</hi> for suffering, not for service; born to be always dying. Shall we complain of one wearisome night, or one fit of illness, who perhaps for many years have scarcely known what it has been to be a day sick, when many others, better than we, have scarcely known what it has been to be a day well? Mr. Baxter's note on this passage is very affecting: "How great a mercy was it to live thirty-eight years under God's wholesome discipline! O my God," saith he, "I thank thee for the like discipline of fifty-eight years; how safe a life is this, in comparison of full prosperity and pleasure!" <div eID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26976" type="x-p"/> IV. The cure and the circumstances of it briefly related, <reference osisRef="John.5.6-John.5.9">v. 6-9</reference>. <div eID="gen26976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26977" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Jesus saw him lie.</hi> Observe, When Christ came up to Jerusalem he visited not the palaces, but the hospitals, which is an instance of his humility, and condescension, and tender compassion, and an <hi type="italic">indication</hi> of his great design in coming into the world, which was to seek and save the sick and wounded. There was a great multitude of poor cripples here at Bethesda, but Christ fastened his eye upon this one, and singled him out from the rest, because he was <hi type="italic">senior</hi> of the house, and in a more deplorable condition than any of the rest; and Christ delights to help the helpless, and hath mercy <hi type="italic">on whom he will have mercy.</hi> Perhaps his companions in tribulation insulted over him, because he had often been disappointed of a cure; therefore Christ took him for his patient: it is his honour to side with the weakest, and bear up those whom he sees <hi type="italic">run down.</hi> <div eID="gen26977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26978" type="x-p"/> 2. He knew and considered <hi type="italic">how long he had lain</hi> in this condition. Those that have been long in affliction may comfort themselves with this, that God keeps account <hi type="italic">how long,</hi> and knows our frame. <div eID="gen26978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> 3. He asked him, <hi type="italic">Wilt thou be made whole?</hi> A strange question to be asked one that had been so long ill. Some indeed would not be made whole, because their sores serve them to beg by and serve them for an excuse for idleness; but this poor man was as unable to <hi type="italic">go a begging</hi> as to <hi type="italic">work,</hi> yet Christ put it to him, (1.) To <hi type="italic">express</hi> his own pity and concern for him. Christ is tenderly inquisitive concerning the desires of those that are in affliction, and is willing to know <hi type="italic">what is their petition:</hi> "What shall I do for you?" (2.) To try him whether he would be beholden for a cure to him against whom the great people were so prejudiced and sought to prejudice others. (3.) To teach him to value the mercy, and to excite in him desires after it. In spiritual cases, people are not willing to be cured of their sins, are loth to part with them. If this point therefore were but gained, if people were willing to be <hi type="italic">made whole,</hi> the work were half done, for Christ is willing to heal, if we be but willing to be healed, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.3">Matt. viii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26980" type="x-p"/> 4. The poor impotent man takes this opportunity to renew his complaint, and to set forth the misery of his case, which makes his cure the more illustrious: <hi type="italic">Sir, I have no man to put me into the pool,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.7">v. 7</reference>. He seems to take Christ's question as an imputation of carelessness and neglect: "If thou hadst had a mind to be healed, thou wouldest have looked better to thy hits, and have got into the healing waters long before now." "No, Master," saith the poor man, "It is not for want of a <hi type="italic">good will,</hi> but of a <hi type="italic">good friend,</hi> that I am unhealed. I have done what I could to help myself, but in vain, for no one else will help me." (1.) He does not think of any other way of being cured than by these waters, and desires no other friendship than to be helped into <hi type="italic">them;</hi> therefore, when Christ cured him, his imagination or expectation could not contribute to it, for he thought of no such thing. (2.) He complains for want of friends to help him in: "<hi type="italic">I have no man,</hi> no friend to do me that kindness." One would think that some of those who had been themselves healed should have lent him a hand; but it is common for the poor to be destitute of friends; <hi type="italic">no man careth for their soul.</hi> To the sick and impotent it is as true a piece of charity to work for them as to relieve them; and thus the poor are capable of being charitable to one another, and ought to be so, though we seldom find that they are so; I speak it to their shame. (3.) He bewails his infelicity, that very often when <hi type="italic">he</hi> was coming <hi type="italic">another stepped in before him.</hi> But a step between him and a cure, and yet he continues impotent. None had the charity to say, "Your case is worse than mine, do you go in now, and I will stay till the next time;" for there is no getting over the old maxim, <hi type="italic">Every one for himself.</hi> Having been so often disappointed, he begins to despair, and now is Christ's time to come to his relief; he delights to help in desperate cases. Observe, How mildly this man speaks of the unkindness of those about him, without any peevish reflections. As we should be thankful for the least kindness, so we should be patient under the greatest contempts; and, let our resentments be ever so <hi type="italic">just,</hi> yet our expressions should ever be <hi type="italic">calm.</hi> And observe further, to his praise, that, though he had waited so long in vain, yet still he continued lying by the pool side, hoping that some time or other help would come, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab. ii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen26980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> 5. Our Lord Jesus hereupon cures him with a word speaking, though he neither asked it nor thought of it. Here is, <div eID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26982" type="x-p"/> (1.) The word he said: <hi type="italic">Rise, take up thy bed,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.8">v. 8</reference>. [1.] He is bidden to <hi type="italic">rise and walk;</hi> a strange command to be given to an <hi type="italic">impotent</hi> man, that had been long disabled; but this divine word was to be the vehicle of a divine power; it was a command to the disease to <hi type="italic">be gone,</hi> to nature to <hi type="italic">be strong,</hi> but it is expressed as a command to him to <hi type="italic">bestir himself.</hi> He must <hi type="italic">rise and walk,</hi> that is, attempt to do it, and in the <hi type="italic">essay</hi> he should receive strength to do it. The conversion of a sinner is the cure of a chronic disease; this is ordinarily done by the word, a word of command: Arise, and walk; <hi type="italic">turn, and live; make ye a new heart;</hi> which no more supposes a power in us to do it, without the grace of God, <hi type="italic">distinguishing</hi> grace, than this supposed such a power in the impotent man. But, if he had not attempted to help himself, he had not been cured, and he must have <hi type="italic">borne the blame;</hi> yet it does not therefore follow that, when he did rise and walk, it was by his own strength; no, it was by the power of Christ, and he must have all the glory. Observe, Christ did not bid him rise and go into the waters, but <hi type="italic">rise and walk.</hi> Christ did that for us which the law could not do, and set that aside. [2.] He is bidden to <hi type="italic">take up his bed. First,</hi> To make it to appear that it was a <hi type="italic">perfect cure,</hi> and purely miraculous; for he did not recover strength by degrees, but from the extremity of weakness and impotency he suddenly stepped into the highest degree of bodily strength; so that he was able to carry as great a load as any porter that had been as long <hi type="italic">used</hi> to it as he had been <hi type="italic">disused.</hi> He, who this minute was not able to turn himself in his bed, the next minute was able to carry his bed. The man sick of the palsy (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.6">Matt. ix. 6</reference>) was bidden to <hi type="italic">go to his house,</hi> but probably this man had no house to go to, the hospital was his home; therefore he is bidden to <hi type="italic">rise and walk. Secondly,</hi> It was to <hi type="italic">proclaim</hi> the cure, and make it public; for, being the sabbath day, whoever carried a burden through the streets made himself very remarkable, and every one would enquire what was the meaning of it; thereby notice of the miracle would spread, to the honour of God. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Christ would thus witness against the tradition of the elders, which had stretched the law of the sabbath beyond its intention; and would likewise show that he was <hi type="italic">Lord of the sabbath,</hi> and had power to make what alterations he pleased about it, and to over-rule the law. Joshua, and the host of Israel, marched about Jericho on the sabbath day, when God commanded them, so did this man carry his bed, in obedience to a command. The case may be such that it may become a work of <hi type="italic">necessity,</hi> or <hi type="italic">mercy,</hi> to carry a bed on the sabbath day; but here it was more, it was a work of <hi type="italic">piety,</hi> being designed purely for the glory of God. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He would hereby try the faith and obedience of his patient. By carrying his bed publicly, he exposed himself to the censure of the ecclesiastical court, and was liable, at least, to be <hi type="italic">scourged in the synagogue.</hi> Now, will he run the hazard of this, in obedience to Christ? Yes, he will. Those that have been <hi type="italic">healed by Christ's word</hi> should be <hi type="italic">ruled by his word,</hi> whatever it cost them. <div eID="gen26982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> (2.) The efficacy of this word (<reference osisRef="John.5.9">v. 9</reference>): a divine power went alone with it, and immediately he was <hi type="italic">made whole, took up his bed, and walked.</hi> [1.] He felt the power of Christ's word healing him: <hi type="italic">Immediately he was made whole.</hi> What a joyful surprise was this to the poor cripple, to find himself all of a sudden so easy, so strong, so able to help himself! What a new world was he in, in an instant! Nothing is too hard for Christ to do. [2.] He obeyed the power of Christ's word commanding him. He <hi type="italic">took up his bed and walked,</hi> and did not care who blamed him or threatened him for it. The proof of our spiritual cure is our rising and walking. Hath Christ healed our spiritual diseases? Let us go whithersoever he sends us, and <hi type="italic">take up</hi> whatever he is pleased to lay upon us, and <hi type="italic">walk before him.</hi> <div eID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26984" type="x-p"/> V. What became of the poor man after he was cured. We are here told, <div eID="gen26984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26985" type="x-p"/> 1. What passed between him and the Jews who saw him carry his bed on the sabbath day; for on that day this cure was wrought, and it was the sabbath that fell within the passover week, and therefore a <hi type="italic">high day,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.19.31">ch. xix. 31</reference>. Christ's work was such that he needed not make any difference between sabbath days and other days, for he was always about his Father's business; but he wrought many remarkable cures on that day, perhaps to encourage his church to expect those spiritual favours from him, in their observance of the Christian sabbath, which were typified by his miraculous cures. Now here, <div eID="gen26985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26986" type="x-p"/> (1.) The Jews quarrelled with the man for carrying his bed on the sabbath day, telling him that <hi type="italic">it was not lawful,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.10">v. 10</reference>. It does not appear whether they were magistrates, who had power to <hi type="italic">punish</hi> him, or common people, who could only <hi type="italic">inform</hi> against him; but thus far was commendable, that, while they knew not by <hi type="italic">what authority</hi> he did it, they were jealous for the honour of the sabbath, and could not unconcernedly see it <hi type="italic">profaned;</hi> like Nehemiah. <reference osisRef="Neh.13.17">Neh. xiii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen26986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> (2.) The man justified himself in what he did by a warrant that would bear him out, <reference osisRef="John.5.11">v. 11</reference>. "I do not do it in contempt of the law and the sabbath, but in obedience to one who, by <hi type="italic">making me whole,</hi> has given me an undeniable proof that he is greater than either. He that could work such a miracle as to <hi type="italic">make me whole</hi> no doubt might give me such a command as to carry <hi type="italic">my bed;</hi> he that could overrule the powers of nature no doubt might overrule a positive law, especially in an instance not of the essence of the law. He that was so kind as to make me whole would not be so unkind as to bid me do what is sinful." Christ, by curing another paralytic, proved his power to <hi type="italic">forgive sin,</hi> here to <hi type="italic">give law;</hi> if his pardons are valid, his edicts are so, and his miracles prove both. <div eID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> (3.) The Jews enquired further who it was that gave him this warrant (<reference osisRef="John.5.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">What man is that?</hi> Observe, How industriously they <hi type="italic">overlooked</hi> that which might be a ground of their <hi type="italic">faith in Christ.</hi> They enquire not, no, not for curiosity, "Who is it that <hi type="italic">made thee whole?</hi>" While they industriously caught at that which might be a ground of reflection upon Christ (<hi type="italic">What man is</hi> it who said unto thee, <hi type="italic">Take up thy bed?</hi>) they would fain <hi type="italic">subpoena</hi> the patient to be witness against his physician, and to be his betrayer. In their question, observe, [1.] They resolve to look upon Christ as a <hi type="italic">mere man: What man is that?</hi> For, though he gave ever such convincing proofs of it, they were resolved that they would never own him to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> [2.] They resolve to look upon him as a bad <hi type="italic">man,</hi> and take it for granted that he who bade this man carry his bed, whatever divine commission he might <hi type="italic">produce,</hi> was certainly a delinquent, and as such they resolve to prosecute him. <hi type="italic">What man is that</hi> who durst give such orders? <div eID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> (4.) The poor man was unable to give them any account of him: <hi type="italic">He wist not who he was,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.13">v. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ was <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> to him when he healed him. Probably he had heard of the name of Jesus, but had never seen him, and therefore could not tell that this was he. Note, Christ does many a good turn for those that know him not, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4-Isa.45.5">Isa. xlv. 4, 5</reference>. He enlightens, strengthens, quickens, comforts us, and we <hi type="italic">wist not who he is;</hi> nor are aware how much we receive daily by his mediation. This man, being unacquainted with Christ, could not actually believe in him for a cure; but Christ knew the dispositions of his soul, and suited his favours to them, as to the blind man in a like case, <reference osisRef="John.9.36">ch. ix. 36</reference>. Our covenant and communion with God take rise, not so much from our knowledge of him, as from his knowledge of us. We <hi type="italic">know God,</hi> or, rather, are <hi type="italic">known of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> [2.] For the present he <hi type="italic">kept himself unknown;</hi> for as soon as he had wrought the cure he <hi type="italic">conveyed himself away,</hi> he <hi type="italic">made himself unknown</hi> (so some read it), <hi type="italic">a multitude being in that place.</hi> This is mentioned to show, either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How Christ conveyed himself away—by retiring into the crowd, so as not to be distinguished from a common person. He that was the chief of ten thousand often made himself one of the throng. It is sometimes the lot of those who have by their services signalized themselves to be levelled with the multitude, and overlooked. Or <hi type="italic">Secondly, Why</hi> he conveyed himself away, because there was <hi type="italic">a multitude</hi> there, and he industriously avoided both the <hi type="italic">applause</hi> of those who would admire the miracle and <hi type="italic">cry that up,</hi> and the censure of those who would censure him as a sabbath-breaker, and <hi type="italic">run him down.</hi> Those that are active for God in their generation must expect to pass through <hi type="italic">evil report</hi> and <hi type="italic">good report;</hi> and it is wisdom as much as may be to keep out of the hearing of both; lest by the one we be <hi type="italic">exalted,</hi> and by the other <hi type="italic">depressed,</hi> above measure. Christ left the miracle to commend itself, and the man on whom it was wrought to justify it. <div eID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26992" type="x-p"/> 2. What passed between him and our Lord Jesus at their next interview, <reference osisRef="John.5.14">v. 14</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen26992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26993" type="x-p"/> (1.) Where Christ found him: <hi type="italic">in the temple,</hi> the place of public worship. In our attendance on public worship we may expect to meet with Christ, and improve our acquaintance with him. Observe, [1.] Christ <hi type="italic">went to the temple.</hi> Though he had many enemies, yet he appeared in public, because there he bore his testimony to divine institutions, and had opportunity of doing good. [2.] The man that was cured <hi type="italic">went to the temple.</hi> There Christ found him the same day, as it should seem, that he was healed; thither he straightway went, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because he had, <hi type="italic">by his infirmity,</hi> been so long <hi type="italic">detained</hi> thence. Perhaps he had not been there for thirty-eight years, and therefore, as soon as ever the embargo is taken off, his first visit shall be to the temple, as Hezekiah intimates his shall be (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">Isa. xxxviii. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord? Secondly,</hi> Because he had <hi type="italic">by his recovery</hi> a good errand thither; he went up to the temple to return thanks to God for his recovery. When God has at any time restored us our health we ought to attend him with solemn praises (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.18-Ps.116.19">Ps. cxvi. 18, 19</reference>), and the sooner the better, while the sense of the mercy is fresh. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Because he had, by <hi type="italic">carrying his bed,</hi> seemed to put a contempt on the sabbath, he would thus show that he had an honour for it, and made conscience of sabbath-sanctification, in that on which the chief stress of it is laid, which is the <hi type="italic">public worship</hi> of God. Works of necessity and mercy are allowed; but when they are over we must <hi type="italic">go to the temple.</hi> <div eID="gen26993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he said to him. When Christ has cured us, he has not done with us; he now applies himself to the healing of his soul, and this <hi type="italic">by the word</hi> too. [1.] He gives him a <hi type="italic">memento</hi> of his cure: <hi type="italic">Behold thou art made whole.</hi> He found himself made whole, yet Christ calls his attention to it. <hi type="italic">Behold, consider</hi> it seriously, how sudden, how strange, how cheap, how easy, the cure was: <hi type="italic">admire it;</hi> behold, and wonder: <hi type="italic">Remember it;</hi> let the impressions of it abide, and never be lost, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Isa. xxxviii. 9</reference>. [2.] He gives him a caution against sin, in consideration hereof, <hi type="italic">Being made whole, sin no more.</hi> This implies that his disease was the punishment of sin; whether of some remarkably flagrant sin, or only of sin in general, we cannot tell, but we know that sin is the procuring cause of sickness, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.17-Ps.107.18">Ps. cvii. 17, 18</reference>. Some observe that Christ did not make mention of sin to any of his patients, except to this <hi type="italic">impotent</hi> man, and another who was in like manner diseased, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.5">Mark ii. 5</reference>. While those chronical diseases lasted, they prevented the outward acts of many sins, and therefore watchfulness was the more necessary when the disability was removed. Christ intimates that those who are <hi type="italic">made whole,</hi> who are eased of the present sensible punishment of sin, are in danger of <hi type="italic">returning</hi> to sin when the terror and restraint are over, unless divine grace dry up the fountain. When the trouble which only dammed up the current is over, the waters will return to their old course; and therefore there is great need of watchfulness, lest after healing mercy we return again to folly. The <hi type="italic">misery</hi> we were <hi type="italic">made whole from</hi> warns us to sin no more, having felt the smart of sin; the <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> we were <hi type="italic">made whole by</hi> is an engagement upon us not to offend him who healed us. This is the voice of every providence, <hi type="italic">Go and sin no more.</hi> This man began his new life very hopefully <hi type="italic">in the temple,</hi> yet Christ saw it necessary to give him this caution; for it is common for people, when they are sick, to <hi type="italic">promise much,</hi> when newly recovered to <hi type="italic">perform something,</hi> but after awhile to <hi type="italic">forget all.</hi> [3.] He gives him warning of his danger, in case he should return to his former sinful course: <hi type="italic">Lest a worse thing come to thee.</hi> Christ, who knows all men's hearts, knew that he was one of those that must be <hi type="italic">frightened</hi> from sin. Thirty-eight years' lameness, one would think, was a thing bad enough; yet there is something <hi type="italic">worse</hi> that will come to him if he relapse into sin after God has <hi type="italic">given him such a deliverance</hi> as this, <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.13-Ezra.9.14">Ezra ix. 13, 14</reference>. The hospital where he lay was a melancholy place, but hell is much more so: the doom of apostates is a worse thing than thirty-eight years' lameness. <div eID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26995" type="x-p"/> VI. Now, after this interview between Christ and his patient, observe in the <reference osisRef="John.5.15-John.5.16">two following verses</reference>, 1. The notice which the poor simple man gave to the Jews concerning Christ, <reference osisRef="John.5.15">v. 15</reference>. He told them it was Jesus that had <hi type="italic">made him whole.</hi> We have reason to think that he intended this for the honour of Christ and the benefit of the Jews, little thinking that he who had so much power and goodness could have <hi type="italic">any</hi> enemies; but those who wish well to Christ's kingdom must have the <hi type="italic">wisdom of the serpent,</hi> lest they do more hurt than good with their zeal, and must not cast pearls before swine. 2. The rage and enmity of the Jews against him: <hi type="italic">Therefore did the</hi> rulers of the Jews <hi type="italic">persecute Jesus.</hi> See, (1.) How absurd and unreasonable their enmity to Christ was. <hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because he had made a poor sick man well, and so eased the public charge, upon which, it is likely, he had subsisted; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they persecuted him, because he did good in Israel. (2.) How bloody and cruel it was: <hi type="italic">They sought to slay him;</hi> nothing less than his blood, his life, would satisfy them. (3.) How it was varnished over with a colour of zeal for the honour of the sabbath; for this was the pretended crime, <hi type="italic">Because he had done these things on the sabbath day,</hi> as if that circumstance were enough to vitiate the best and most divine actions, and to render <hi type="italic">him</hi> obnoxious whose deeds were otherwise most meritorious. Thus hypocrites often cover their real enmity against the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of godliness with a pretended zeal for the <hi type="italic">form</hi> of it.
entries.98752cef7f9d3f7f4c74e348640a3e34e48cedaf: <div eID="gen26995" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Jews; All Judgment Committed to Christ; The Christian Charter.</title> <div sID="gen26996" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> But Jesus answered them, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work. <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then answered Jesus and said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise. <hi type="super">20</hi> For the Father loveth the Son, and showeth him all things that himself doeth: and he will show him greater works than these, that ye may marvel. <hi type="super">21</hi> For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth <hi type="italic">them;</hi> even so the Son quickeneth whom he will. <hi type="super">22</hi> For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son: <hi type="super">23</hi> That all <hi type="italic">men</hi> should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him. <hi type="super">24</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life. <hi type="super">25</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live. <hi type="super">26</hi> For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself; <hi type="super">27</hi> And hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man. <hi type="super">28</hi> Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, <hi type="super">29</hi> And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation. <hi type="super">30</hi> I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me. <div eID="gen26996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26997" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's discourse upon occasion of his being accused as a sabbath-breaker, and it seems to be his vindication of himself before the sanhedrim, when he was arraigned before them: whether on the same day, or two or three days after, does not appear; probably the same day. Observe, <div eID="gen26997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26998" type="x-p"/> I. The doctrine laid down, by which he justified what he did on the sabbath day (<reference osisRef="John.5.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">He answered them.</hi> This supposes that he had something laid to his charge: or what they suggested one to another, when they sought to slay him (<reference osisRef="John.5.16">v. 16</reference>), he <hi type="italic">knew,</hi> and gave this reply to, <hi type="italic">My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.</hi> At other times, in answer to the like charge, he had pleaded the example of David's eating the show-bread, of the priests' slaying the sacrifices, and of the people's watering their cattle on the sabbath day; but here he goes higher and alleges the example of his Father and his divine authority; waiving all other pleas, he insists upon that which was <hi type="italic">instar omnium—equivalent to the whole,</hi> and abides by it, which he had mentioned, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.8">Matt. xii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath day;</hi> but he here enlarges on it. 1. He pleads that he was the Son of God, <hi type="italic">plainly intimated in his calling God his Father;</hi> and, if so, his holiness was <hi type="italic">unquestionable</hi> and his sovereignty <hi type="italic">incontestable;</hi> and he might make what alterations he pleased of the divine law. <hi type="italic">Surely they will reverence the Son,</hi> the heir of all things. 2. That he was a worker together with God. (1.) <hi type="italic">My Father worketh hitherto.</hi> The example of God's resting on the seventh day from all his work is, in the fourth commandment, made the ground of our observing it as a <hi type="italic">sabbath</hi> or <hi type="italic">day of rest.</hi> Now God rested only from such work as he had done the six days before; otherwise he <hi type="italic">worketh hitherto,</hi> he is every day working, sabbath days and week-days, upholding and governing all the creatures, and concurring by his common providence to all the motions and operations of nature, <hi type="italic">to his own glory;</hi> therefore, when we are appointed to rest on the sabbath day, yet we are not restrained from doing that which has a direct tendency <hi type="italic">to the glory of God,</hi> as the man's carrying his bed had. (2.) <hi type="italic">I work;</hi> not only therefore I <hi type="italic">may</hi> work, <hi type="italic">like him,</hi> in doing good on sabbath days as well as other days, but I also <hi type="italic">work with him.</hi> As God created all things by Christ, so he supports and governs all by him, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. This sets what he does above all exception; he that is so great a worker must needs be an uncontrollable governor; he that does all is Lord of all, and therefore <hi type="italic">Lord of the sabbath,</hi> which particular branch of his authority he would now assert, because he was shortly to show it further, in the change of the day from the seventh to the first. <div eID="gen26998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26999" type="x-p"/> II. The offence that was taken at his doctrine (<reference osisRef="John.5.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Jews sought the more to kill him.</hi> His defence was made his offence, as if by justifying himself he had made bad worse. Note, Those that will not be enlightened by the word of Christ will be enraged and exasperated by it, and nothing more vexes the enemies of Christ than his asserting his authority; see <reference osisRef="Ps.2.3-Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 3-5</reference>. They sought to kill him, <div eID="gen26999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27000" type="x-p"/> 1. Because he had broken the sabbath; for, let him say what he would in his own justification, they are resolved, right or wrong, to <hi type="italic">find him guilty</hi> of sabbath breaking. When malice and envy sit upon the bench, reason and justice may even be silent at the bar, for whatever they can say will undoubtedly be over-ruled. <div eID="gen27000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27001" type="x-p"/> 2. Not only so, but he had said also <hi type="italic">that God was his Father.</hi> Now they pretend a jealousy for <hi type="italic">God's honour,</hi> as before for the sabbath day, and charge Christ with it as a heinous crime that he made himself equal with God; and a heinous crime it had been if he had not really been so. It was the sin of Lucifer, <hi type="italic">I will be like the Most High.</hi> Now, (1.) This was justly inferred from what he said, that he was the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> and that God was <hi type="italic">his Father,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">patera idion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">his own Father;</hi> his, so as he was no one's else. He had said that he worked with his Father, by the same authority and power, and hereby he made himself equal with God. <hi type="italic">Ecce intelligunt Judæi, quod non intelligunt Ariani—Behold, the Jews understand what the Arians do not.</hi> (2.) Yet it was unjustly imputed to him as an offence that he equalled himself with God, for he was and is God, equal with the Father (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.6">Phil. ii. 6</reference>); and therefore Christ, in answer to this charge, does not except against the innuendo as strained or forced, makes out his claim and proves that he is equal with God in power and glory. <div eID="gen27001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27002" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's discourse upon this occasion, which continues without interruption to the end of the chapter. In <reference osisRef="John.5.19-John.5.47">these verses</reference> he explains, and afterwards confirms, his commission, as Mediator and plenipotentiary in the treaty between God and man. And, as the honours he is hereby <hi type="italic">entitled to</hi> are such as it is not fit for any creature to receive, so the work he is hereby entrusted with is such as it is not possible for any creature to go through with, and therefore he is God, equal with the Father. <div eID="gen27002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">In general.</hi> He is one with the Father in all he does as Mediator, and there was a perfectly good understanding between them in the whole matter. It is ushered in with a solemn preface (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you;</hi> I the Amen, the Amen, say it. This intimates that the things declared are, (1.) Very awful and great, and such as should command the most serious attention. (2.) Very sure, and such as should command an unfeigned assent. (3.) That they are matters purely of divine revelation; things which Christ has told us, and which we could not otherwise have come to the knowledge of. Two things he saith in general concerning the Son's oneness with the Father in working:— <div eID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> [1.] That the Son <hi type="italic">conforms to the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Son can do nothing of himself but what he sees the Father do;</hi> for <hi type="italic">these things does the Son.</hi> The Lord Jesus, as Mediator, is <hi type="italic">First, Obedient to his Father's will;</hi> so entirely obedient that he <hi type="italic">can do nothing of himself,</hi> in the same sense as it is said, <hi type="italic">God cannot</hi> lie, <hi type="italic">cannot deny</hi> himself, which expresses the perfection of his truth, not any imperfection in his strength; so here, Christ was so entirely devoted to his Father's will that it was impossible for him in any thing to act separately. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">observant of his Father's counsel;</hi> he can, he will, do nothing <hi type="italic">but what he sees the Father do.</hi> No man can <hi type="italic">find out the work of God,</hi> but the only-begotten Son, who lay in his bosom, sees what he does, is intimately acquainted with his purposes, and has the plan of them ever before him. What he did as Mediator, throughout his whole undertaking, was the exact transcript or counterpart of what the Father did; that is, what he designed, when he formed the plan of our redemption in his eternal counsels, and settled those measures in every thing which never could be <hi type="italic">broken,</hi> nor ever needed to be <hi type="italic">altered.</hi> It was the copy of that <hi type="italic">great original;</hi> it was Christ's faithfulness, as it was Moses's, that he did all <hi type="italic">according to the pattern shown him in the mount.</hi> This is expressed in the present tense, what he <hi type="italic">sees the Father do,</hi> for the same reason that, when he was here upon earth, it was said, He <hi type="italic">is</hi> in heaven (<reference osisRef="John.3.13">ch. iii. 13</reference>), and <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the bosom of the Father (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>); as he was even then by his divine nature present in heaven, so the things done in heaven were <hi type="italic">present</hi> to his knowledge. What the Father did in his counsels, the Son had ever in his view, and still he had his eye upon it, as David in spirit spoke of him, <hi type="italic">I have set the Lord always before me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Ps. xvi. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Yet he is <hi type="italic">equal</hi> with the Father in <hi type="italic">working;</hi> for <hi type="italic">what things soever</hi> the Father does <hi type="italic">these also does the Son likewise;</hi> he did the <hi type="italic">same</hi> things, not <hi type="italic">such</hi> things, but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tauta</hi></hi>, the <hi type="italic">same</hi> things; and he did them in the <hi type="italic">same manner,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">homoios</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">likewise,</hi> with the same authority, and liberty, and wisdom, the same energy and efficacy. Does the Father enact, repeal, and alter, positive laws? Does he over-rule the course of nature, know men's hearts? So does the Son. The power of the Mediator is a divine power. <div eID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> [2.] That the Father <hi type="italic">communicates</hi> to the Son, <reference osisRef="John.5.20">v. 20</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27006" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The inducement to it: <hi type="italic">The Father loveth the Son;</hi> he declared, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> He had not only a good will to the undertaking, but an infinite complacency in the undertaker. Christ was now hated of men, one whom the nation abhorred (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">Isa. xlix. 7</reference>); but he comforted himself with this, that his Father loved him. <div eID="gen27006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27007" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The instances of it. He shows it, 1. In what he <hi type="italic">does</hi> communicate to him: <hi type="italic">He shows him all things that himself doth.</hi> The Father's measures in making and ruling the world are shown to the Son, that he may take the same measures in framing and governing the church, which work was to be a duplicate of the work of creation and providence, and it is therefore called <hi type="italic">the world to come.</hi> He shows him all things <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ha autos poiei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">which he does,</hi> that is, which the <hi type="italic">Son</hi> does, so it might be construed; all that the Son does is by direction from the Father; he <hi type="italic">shows</hi> him. 2. In what he <hi type="italic">will</hi> communicate; he will <hi type="italic">show him,</hi> that is, will appoint and direct him to do <hi type="italic">greater works than these.</hi> (1.) Works of greater <hi type="italic">power</hi> than the <hi type="italic">curing of the impotent man;</hi> for he should raise the dead, and should himself rise from the dead. By the power of nature, with the use of means, a disease may possibly in time be cured; but nature can never, by the use of any means, in any time raise the dead. (2.) Works of greater <hi type="italic">authority</hi> than warranting the man to <hi type="italic">carry his bed on the sabbath day.</hi> They thought this a daring attempt; but what was this to his abrogating the whole ceremonial law, and instituting new ordinances, which he would shortly do, "<hi type="italic">that you may marvel!</hi>" Now they looked upon his works with contempt and indignation, but he will shortly do that which they will look upon with amazement, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.16">Luke vii. 16</reference>. Many are brought to marvel at Christ's works, whereby he has the honour of them, who are not brought to believe, by which they would have the benefit of them. <div eID="gen27007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27008" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">In particular.</hi> He proves his equality with the Father, by specifying some of those works which he does that are the peculiar works of God. This is enlarged upon, <reference osisRef="John.5.21-John.5.30">v. 21-30</reference>. He does, and shall do, that which is the peculiar work of God's sovereign dominion and jurisdiction—<hi type="italic">judging</hi> and <hi type="italic">executing judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.22-John.5.24">v. 22-24</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. These two are interwoven, as being nearly connected; and what is said once is repeated and inculcated; put both together, and they will prove that Christ said not amiss when he made himself <hi type="italic">equal with God.</hi> <div eID="gen27008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27009" type="x-p"/> (1.) Observe what is here said concerning the Mediator's power to <hi type="italic">raise the dead</hi> and <hi type="italic">give life.</hi> See [1.] His <hi type="italic">authority</hi> to do it (<reference osisRef="John.5.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the Father raiseth up the dead,</hi> so <hi type="italic">the Son quickeneth whom he will. First,</hi> It is God's prerogative to raise the dead, and give life, even his who first <hi type="italic">breathed</hi> into man the <hi type="italic">breath of life,</hi> and so made him a <hi type="italic">living soul;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deut. xxxii. 30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.6">1 Sam. ii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.20">Ps. lxviii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Rom. iv. 17</reference>. This God had done by the prophets Elijah and Elisha, and it was a confirmation of their mission. A <hi type="italic">resurrection from the dead</hi> never lay in the common road of nature, nor ever fell within the thought of those that studied only the compass of nature's power, one of whose received axioms was point blank against it: <hi type="italic">A privatione ad habitum non datur regressus—Existence, when once extinguished, cannot be rekindled.</hi> It was therefore ridiculed at Athens as an <hi type="italic">absurd</hi> thing, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.32">Acts xvii. 32</reference>. It is purely the work of a divine power, and the knowledge of it purely by divine revelation. This the Jews would own. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The Mediator is invested with this prerogative: <hi type="italic">He quickens whom he will;</hi> raises to life whom he pleases, and when he pleases. He does not enliven things by natural necessity, as the sun does, whose beams revive of course; but he acts as a free agent, has the dispensing of his power in his own hand, and is never either <hi type="italic">con</hi>strained, or <hi type="italic">re</hi>strained, in the use of it. As he has the power, so he has the wisdom and sovereignty, of a God; has the <hi type="italic">key of the grave and of death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Rev. i. 18</reference>), not as a servant, to open and shut as he is bidden, for he has it as the <hi type="italic">key of David,</hi> which he is master of, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.7">Rev. iii. 7</reference>. An absolute prince is described by this (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.19">Dan. v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whom he would he slew or kept alive;</hi> it is true of Christ without hyperbole. <div eID="gen27009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27010" type="x-p"/> [2.] His <hi type="italic">ability</hi> to do it. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he has power to quicken whom he will as the Father does, because <hi type="italic">he has life in himself, as the Father has,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.26">v. 26</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is certain that the Father <hi type="italic">has life in himself.</hi> Not only he is a <hi type="italic">self-existent</hi> Being, who does not derive from, or depend upon, any other (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Exod. iii. 14</reference>), but he is a sovereign giver of life; he has the disposal of life in himself; and of all good (for so <hi type="italic">life</hi> sometimes signifies); it is all derived from him, and dependent on him. He is to his creatures the fountain of life, and all good; author of their being and well-being; the living God, and the God of all living. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is as certain that he has <hi type="italic">given to the Son to have life in himself.</hi> As the Father is the original of all natural life and good, being the great Creator, so the Son, as Redeemer, is the original of all spiritual life and good; is that to the church which the Father is to the world; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.6">1 Cor. viii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col. i. 19</reference>. The kingdom of grace, and all the life in that kingdom, are as fully and absolutely in the hand of the Redeemer as the kingdom of providence is in the hand of the Creator; and as God, who gives being to all things, has his being of himself, so Christ, who gives life, raised himself to life by his own power, <reference osisRef="John.10.18">ch. x. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen27010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27011" type="x-p"/> [3.] His <hi type="italic">acting</hi> according to this authority and ability. Having <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> and being authorized to <hi type="italic">quicken whom he will,</hi> by virtue hereof there are, accordingly, two resurrections performed by his powerful word, both which are here spoken of:— <div eID="gen27011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27012" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A resurrection that <hi type="italic">now is</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.29">v. 29</reference>), a resurrection from the death of sin to the life of righteousness, by the power of Christ's grace. <hi type="italic">The hour is coming, and now is.</hi> It is a resurrection begun already, and further to be carried on, <hi type="italic">when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God.</hi> This is plainly distinguished from that in <reference osisRef="John.5.28">v. 28</reference>, which speaks of the resurrection at the end of time. This says nothing, as that does, of the dead in their graces, and of all of them, and their coming forth. Now, 1. Some think this was fulfilled in those whom he miraculously raised to life, Jairus's daughter, the widow's son, and Lazarus; and it is observable that all whom Christ raised were <hi type="italic">spoken to,</hi> as, <hi type="italic">Damsel, arise; Young man, arise; Lazarus, come forth;</hi> whereas those raised under the Old Testament were raised, not by a word, but other applications, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.21">1 Kings xvii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.34">2 Kings iv. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.21">xiii. 21</reference>. Some understand it of those saints that rose with Christ; but we do not read of the <hi type="italic">voice of the Son of God</hi> calling them. But, 2. I rather understand it of the power of the doctrine of Christ, for the recovering and quickening of those that were <hi type="italic">dead in trespasses and sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Eph. ii. 1</reference>. The <hi type="italic">hour</hi> was <hi type="italic">coming</hi> when dead souls should be made alive by the <hi type="italic">preaching</hi> of the gospel, and a spirit of life from God accompanying it: nay, it <hi type="italic">then was,</hi> while Christ was upon earth. It may refer especially to the <hi type="italic">calling of the Gentiles,</hi> which is said to be as life from the dead, and, some think, was prefigured by Ezekiel's vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1">ch. xxxvii. 1</reference>), and foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa. xxvi. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thy dead men shall live.</hi> But it is to be applied to all the wonderful success of the gospel, among both Jews and Gentiles; an hour which still <hi type="italic">is,</hi> and is still <hi type="italic">coming,</hi> till all the elect be effectually called. Note, (1.) Sinners are spiritually <hi type="italic">dead,</hi> destitute of spiritual life, sense, strength, and motion, dead to God, miserable, but neither sensible of their misery nor able to help themselves out of it. (2.) The conversion of a soul to God is its resurrection from death to life; then it begins to live when it begins to <hi type="italic">live to God,</hi> to breathe after him, and move towards him. (3.) It is by the <hi type="italic">voice of the Son of God</hi> that souls are raised to spiritual life; it is wrought by his power, and that power conveyed and communicated by his word: <hi type="italic">The dead shall hear,</hi> shall be made to hear, to understand, receive, and believe, the <hi type="italic">voice of the Son of God,</hi> to hear it as his voice; then the Spirit by it gives life, otherwise the <hi type="italic">letter kills.</hi> (4.) The voice of Christ must be heard by us, that we may live by it. They that hear, and attend to what they hear, shall live. <hi type="italic">Hear and your soul shall live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen27012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27013" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A resurrection yet <hi type="italic">to come;</hi> this is spoken of, <reference osisRef="John.5.28-John.5.29">v. 28, 29</reference>, introduced with, "<hi type="italic">Marvel not at this,</hi> which I have said of the <hi type="italic">first</hi> resurrection, do not reject it as incredible and absurd, for at the end of time you shall all see a more sensible and amazing proof of the power and authority of the Son of man." As <hi type="italic">his own</hi> resurrection was reserved to be the final and concluding proof of his personal commission, so the resurrection of <hi type="italic">all men</hi> is reserved to be a like proof of his commission to be executed by his spirit. Now observe here, <div eID="gen27013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27014" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> When this resurrection shall be: <hi type="italic">The hour is coming;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">fixed</hi> to an hour, so very punctual is this great appointment. The judgment is not adjourned <hi type="italic">sine die—to some time not yet pitched upon;</hi> no, <hi type="italic">he hath appointed a day. The hour is coming.</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) It is <hi type="italic">not yet</hi> come, it is not the hour spoken of at <reference osisRef="John.5.25">v. 25</reference>, that is coming, and <hi type="italic">now is.</hi> Those erred dangerously who said that the <hi type="italic">resurrection was past already,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2 Tim. ii. 18</reference>, But, (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It <hi type="italic">will certainly</hi> come, it is coming on, nearer every day than other; it is at the door. How far off it is we know not; but we know that it is infallibly designed and unalterably determined. <div eID="gen27014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Who shall be raised: <hi type="italic">All that are in the graves,</hi> all that have died from the beginning of time, and all that shall die to the end of time. It was said (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Many</hi> shall arise; Christ here tells us that those <hi type="italic">many</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">all; all</hi> must appear before the Judge, and therefore <hi type="italic">all</hi> must be raised; every person, and the whole of every person; every soul shall return to its body, and every <hi type="italic">bone to its bone.</hi> The grave is the prison of dead bodies, where they are <hi type="italic">detained;</hi> their furnace, where they are <hi type="italic">consumed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.24.19">Job xxiv. 19</reference>); yet, in prospect of their resurrection, we may call it their <hi type="italic">bed,</hi> where they sleep to be <hi type="italic">awaked</hi> again; their treasury, where they are laid up to be used again. Even those that are not <hi type="italic">put into graves</hi> shall arise; but, because most are put into graves, Christ uses this expression, <hi type="italic">all that are in the graves.</hi> The Jews used the word <hi type="italic">sheol</hi> for the <hi type="italic">grave,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">the state of the dead;</hi> all that are in that state <hi type="italic">shall hear.</hi> <div eID="gen27015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> How they shall be raised. Two things are here told us:—(<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The efficient of this resurrection: <hi type="italic">They shall hear his voice;</hi> that is, he shall cause them to hear it, as Lazarus was made to hear that word, <hi type="italic">Come forth;</hi> a divine power shall go along with the voice, to put life into them, and enable them to obey it. When Christ rose, there was no voice heard, not a word spoken, because he rose by his own power; but at the resurrection of the children of men we find three voices spoken of, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1 Thess. iv. 16</reference>. The Lord shall descend with a <hi type="italic">shout,</hi> the shout of a king, with <hi type="italic">the voice of the archangel;</hi> either Christ himself, the prince of the angels, or the commander-in-chief, under him, of the heavenly hosts; and with <hi type="italic">the trumpet of God:</hi> the soldier's trumpet sounding the alarm of war, the judge's trumpet publishing the summons to the court. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The effect of it: <hi type="italic">They shall come forth</hi> out of their graves, as prisoners out of their prison-house; they shall <hi type="italic">arise out</hi> of the dust, and shake themselves from it; see <reference osisRef="Isa.52.1-Isa.52.2">Isa. lii. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.11">11</reference>. But this is not all; they shall <hi type="italic">appear</hi> before Christ's tribunal, shall <hi type="italic">come forth</hi> as those that are to be tried, <hi type="italic">come forth</hi> to the bar, publicly to receive their doom. <div eID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27017" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">d.</hi> To what they shall be raised; to a different state of happiness or misery, according to their different character; to a state of retribution, according to what they did in the state of probation. <div eID="gen27017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27018" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) <hi type="italic">They that have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life;</hi> they shall live again, to live for ever. Note, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] Whatever name men are called by, or whatever plausible profession they make, it will be well in the great day with those only that have <hi type="italic">done good,</hi> have done that which is pleasing to God and profitable to others. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The resurrection of the body will be a resurrection of life to all those, and those only, that have been sincere and constant in <hi type="italic">doing good.</hi> They shall not only be publicly <hi type="italic">acquitted,</hi> as a pardoned criminal, we say, has <hi type="italic">his life,</hi> but they shall be <hi type="italic">admitted</hi> into the presence of God, and that is life, it is better than life; they shall be <hi type="italic">attended</hi> with comforts in perfection. To live is to be <hi type="italic">happy,</hi> and they shall be <hi type="italic">advanced</hi> above the fear of death; that is <hi type="italic">life</hi> indeed in which <hi type="italic">mortality</hi> is for ever <hi type="italic">swallowed</hi> up. <div eID="gen27018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) <hi type="italic">They that have done evil to the resurrection of damnation;</hi> they shall live again, to be for ever dying. The Pharisees thought that the resurrection pertained only to the just, but Christ here rectifies that mistake. Note, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] <hi type="italic">Evil doers,</hi> whatever they pretend, will be treated in the day of judgment as <hi type="italic">evil men.</hi> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The resurrection will be to evil doers, who did not by repentance undo what they had done amiss, a <hi type="italic">resurrection</hi> of damnation. They shall come forth to be publicly convicted of rebellion against God, and publicly <hi type="italic">condemned</hi> to everlasting punishment; to be <hi type="italic">sentenced</hi> to it, and immediately <hi type="italic">sent</hi> to it without reprieve. Such will the resurrection be. <div eID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27020" type="x-p"/> (2.) Observe what is here said concerning the Mediator's <hi type="italic">authority to execute judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.22-John.5.24">v. 22-24</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. As he has an almighty power, so he has a sovereign jurisdiction; and who so fit to preside in the great affairs of the other life as he who is the Father and fountain of life? Here is, <div eID="gen27020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ's commission or delegation to the office of a judge, which is twice spoken of here (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He hath committed all judgment to the Son;</hi> and again (<reference osisRef="John.5.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">he hath given him authority.</hi> <div eID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27022" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">Father judges no man;</hi> not that the Father hath resigned the government, but he is pleased to govern by Jesus Christ; so that man is not under the terror of dealing with God immediately, but has the comfort of access to him by a Mediator. Having made us, he <hi type="italic">may</hi> do what he <hi type="italic">pleases</hi> with us, as the potter with the clay; yet he does not take advantage of this, but draws us <hi type="italic">with the cords of a man.</hi> 2. He does not determine our everlasting condition by the <hi type="italic">covenant of innocency,</hi> nor take the advantage he has against us for the violation of that covenant. The Mediator having undertaken to make a <hi type="italic">vicarious</hi> satisfaction, the matter is referred to him, and God is willing to enter upon a new treaty; <hi type="italic">not under the law</hi> of the Creator, <hi type="italic">but the grace</hi> of the Redeemer. <div eID="gen27022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27023" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly, He has committed all judgment to the Son,</hi> has constituted him <hi type="italic">Lord of all</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.36">Acts x. 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.9">Rom. xiv. 9</reference>), as Joseph in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.40">Gen. xli. 40</reference>. This was prophesied of, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1 Isa.11.3-Isa.11.4 Jer.23.5 Mic.5.1-Mic.5.4">Ps. lxxii. 1; Isa. xii. 3, 4; Jer. xxiii. 5; Mic. v. 1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.67.4">Ps. lxvii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">xcvi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.9">xcviii. 9</reference>. All judgment is committed to our Lord Jesus; for 1. He is <hi type="italic">entrusted</hi> with the administration of the <hi type="italic">providential kingdom,</hi> is <hi type="italic">head over all things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Eph. i. 11</reference>), head of every man, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>. All things consist by him, <reference osisRef="Col.1.17">Col. i. 17</reference>. 2. He is empowered to make laws immediately to bind conscience. <hi type="italic">I say unto you</hi> is now the form in which the statues of the kingdom of heaven run. <hi type="italic">Be it enacted</hi> by the Lord Jesus, and by <hi type="italic">his</hi> authority. All the acts now in force are touched with his sceptre. 3. He is authorized to appoint and settle the terms of the new covenant, and to draw up the articles of peace between God and man; it is God in Christ that reconciles the world, and to him he has given power to confer eternal life. The book of life is the Lamb's book; by his award we must stand or fall. 4. He is commissioned to carry on and complete the war with the powers of darkness; to cast out and <hi type="italic">give judgment against the prince of this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.31">ch. xii. 31</reference>.
