He is commissioned not only to <hi type="italic">judge,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">make war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">Rev. xix. 11</reference>. All that will fight <hi type="italic">for God against Satan</hi> must enlist themselves under <hi type="italic">his</hi> banner. 5. He is constituted sole manager of the judgment of the great day. The ancients generally understood these words of that <hi type="italic">crowning act</hi> of his judicial power. The final and universal judgment is committed to the Son of man; the tribunal is <hi type="italic">his,</hi> it is the judgment-seat of Christ; the retinue is his, <hi type="italic">his</hi> mighty angels; he will try the causes, and pass the sentence. <reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">Acts xvii. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen27023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27024" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He has <hi type="italic">given him authority to execute judgment also,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.27">v. 27</reference>. Observe, 1. What the authority is which our Redeemer is invested with: <hi type="italic">An authority to execute judgment;</hi> he has not only a legislative and judicial power, but an <hi type="italic">executive</hi> power too. The phrase here is used particularly for the judgment of condemnation, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">poiesai krisin</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to execute judgment</hi> upon all; the same with his <hi type="italic">taking vengeance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2 Thess. i. 8</reference>. The ruin of impenitent sinners comes from the hand of Christ; he that <hi type="italic">executes judgment</hi> upon them is the same that would have <hi type="italic">wrought salvation</hi> for them, which makes the sentence unexceptionable; and there is no relief against the sentence of the Redeemer; salvation itself cannot save those whom the Saviour <hi type="italic">condemns,</hi> which makes the ruin <hi type="italic">remediless.</hi> 2. Whence he has that authority: the Father <hi type="italic">gave it to him.</hi> Christ's authority as Mediator is delegated and derived; he acts as the Father's Viceregent, as the Lord's Anointed, the Lord's Christ. Now all this redounds very much to the honour of Christ, acquitting him from the guilt of blasphemy, in making himself <hi type="italic">equal with God;</hi> and very much to the comfort of all believers, who may with the greatest assurance venture their all in such hands. <div eID="gen27024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27025" type="x-p"/> [2.] Here are the reasons (reasons of state) for which this commission was given him. He has all judgment committed to him for two reasons:— <div eID="gen27025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27026" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because he is the <hi type="italic">Son of man;</hi> which denotes these three things:—1. His humiliation and gracious condescension. Man is a worm, the son of man a worm; yet this was the nature, this the character, which the Redeemer assumed, in pursuance of the counsels of love; to this low estate he stooped, and submitted to all the mortifications attending it, because it was <hi type="italic">his Father's will;</hi> in recompence therefore of this wonderful obedience, God did thus dignify him. Because he condescended to be the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> his Father made him <hi type="italic">Lord of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.8-Phil.2.9">Phil. ii. 8, 9</reference>. 2. His affinity and alliance to us. The Father has committed the government of the children of men to him, because, being the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> he is of the same nature with those whom he is <hi type="italic">set over,</hi> and therefore the more unexceptionable, and the more acceptable, as a Judge. <hi type="italic">Their governor shall proceed from the midst of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>. Of this that law was typical; <hi type="italic">One of thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.17.15">Deut. xvii. 15</reference>. 3. His being the Messiah promised. In that famous vision of his kingdom and glory, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14">Dan. vii. 13, 14</reference>, he is called the <hi type="italic">Son of man;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.8.4-Ps.8.6">Ps. viii. 4-6</reference>. Thou has made the Son of man have <hi type="italic">dominion over the works of thy hands.</hi> He is the Messiah, and therefore is invested with all this power. The Jews usually called the Christ the <hi type="italic">Son of David;</hi> but Christ usually called himself the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> which was the more humble title, and bespeaks him a prince and Saviour, not the Jewish nation only, but to the whole race of mankind. <div eID="gen27026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27027" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly, That all men should honour the Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.23">v. 23</reference>. The honouring of Jesus Christ is here spoken of as God's great design (the Son intended to glorify the Father, and therefore the Father intended to glorify the Son, <reference osisRef="John.12.32">ch. xii. 32</reference>); and as man's great duty, in compliance with that design. If God will have the Son honoured, it is the duty of all to whom he is made known to honour him. Observe here, 1. The <hi type="italic">respect</hi> that is to be paid to our Lord Jesus: We must <hi type="italic">honour the Son,</hi> must look upon him as one that is to be <hi type="italic">honoured,</hi> both on account of his transcendent excellences and perfections in himself, and of the relations he stands in to us, and must study to give him honour accordingly; must <hi type="italic">confess that he is Lord,</hi> and worship him; must honour him who was dishonoured for us. 2. The degree of it: <hi type="italic">Even as they honour the Father.</hi> This <hi type="italic">supposes</hi> it to be our duty to <hi type="italic">honour the Father;</hi> for revealed religion is founded on natural religion, and <hi type="italic">directs</hi> us to <hi type="italic">honour the Son,</hi> to honour him with <hi type="italic">divine</hi> honour; we must honour the Redeemer with the same honour with which we honour the Creator. So far was it from blasphemy for him to make himself <hi type="italic">equal with God</hi> that it is the highest injury that can be for us to make him otherwise. The truths and laws of the Christian religion, so far as they are revealed, are as sacred and honourable as those of natural religion, and to be equally had in estimation; for we lie under the same obligations to Christ, the Author of our being; and have as necessary a dependence upon the Redeemer's grace as upon the Creator's providence, which is a sufficient ground for this law—<hi type="italic">to honour the Son as we honour the Father.</hi> To enforce this law, it is added, <hi type="italic">He that honours not the Son honours not the Father</hi> who has sent him. Some pretend a reverence for the Creator, and speak <hi type="italic">honourably</hi> of him, who make light of the Redeemer, and speak <hi type="italic">contemptibly</hi> of him; but let such know that the honours and interests of the Father and Son are so inseparably twisted and interwoven that the Father never reckons himself <hi type="italic">honoured</hi> by any that <hi type="italic">dishonour</hi> the Son. Note, (1.) Indignities done to the Lord Jesus reflect upon God himself, and will so be construed and reckoned for in the court of heaven. The Son having so far espoused the Father's honour as to take <hi type="italic">to himself</hi> the <hi type="italic">reproaches cast on him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Rom. xv. 3</reference>), the Father does no less espouse the Son's honour, and counts himself struck at through him. (2.) The reason of this is because the Son is sent and commissioned by the Father; it is the <hi type="italic">Father who hath sent him.</hi> Affronts to an ambassador are justly resented by the prince that sends him. And by this rule those who truly <hi type="italic">honour the Son honour the Father also;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Phil.2.11">Phil. ii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen27027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27028" type="x-p"/> [3.] Here is the rule by which the Son goes in executing this commission, so those words seem to come in (<reference osisRef="John.5.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that heareth and believeth</hi> hath <hi type="italic">everlasting life.</hi> Here we have the substance of the whole gospel; the preface commands <hi type="italic">attention</hi> to a thing most weighty, and <hi type="italic">assent</hi> to a thing most certain: "<hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you, I,</hi> to whom you hear <hi type="italic">all judgment is committed,</hi> I, in whose lips is a divine sentence; take from <hi type="italic">me</hi> the Christian's <hi type="italic">character</hi> and <hi type="italic">charter.</hi>" <div eID="gen27028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27029" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">character</hi> of a Christian: <hi type="italic">He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me.</hi> To be a Christian indeed is, 1. To <hi type="italic">hear the word of Christ.</hi> It is not enough to be within hearing of it, but we must <hi type="italic">attend on</hi> it, as scholars on the instructions of their teachers; and <hi type="italic">attend to</hi> it, as servants to the commands of their masters; we must hear and obey it, must abide by the gospel of Christ as the fixed rule of our faith and practice. 2. To <hi type="italic">believe on him that sent him;</hi> for Christ's design is to <hi type="italic">bring us to God;</hi> and, as he is the first original of all grace, so is he the last object of all faith. Christ is our <hi type="italic">way;</hi> God is our rest. We must believe on God as <hi type="italic">having sent</hi> Jesus Christ, and recommended himself to our faith and love, by manifesting his glory in <hi type="italic">the face of Jesus Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>), as <hi type="italic">his</hi> Father and <hi type="italic">our Father.</hi> <div eID="gen27029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27030" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">charter</hi> of a Christian, in which all that are Christians indeed are interested. See what we get by Christ. 1. A charter of pardon: <hi type="italic">He shall not come into condemnation.</hi> The grace of the gospel is a full discharge from the curse of the law. A believer shall not only not <hi type="italic">lie under</hi> condemnation eternally, but shall not <hi type="italic">come into condemnation</hi> now, not come into the danger of it (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Rom. viii. 1</reference>), not <hi type="italic">come into judgment,</hi> not be so much as arraigned. 2. A charter of privileges: He is <hi type="italic">passed out of death to life,</hi> is invested in a present happiness in spiritual life and entitled to a future happiness in eternal life. The tenour of the first covenant was, <hi type="italic">Do this and live;</hi> the man that doeth them shall live in them. Now this proves Christ equal with the Father that he has power to propose the <hi type="italic">same</hi> benefit to the <hi type="italic">hearers of his word</hi> that had been proposed to the <hi type="italic">keepers of the old law,</hi> that is, life: <hi type="italic">Hear and live, believe and live,</hi> is what we may venture our souls upon, when we are disabled to <hi type="italic">do and live;</hi> see <reference osisRef="John.17.2">ch. xvii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen27030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27031" type="x-p"/> [4.] Here is the righteousness of his proceedings pursuant to this commission, <reference osisRef="John.5.30">v. 30</reference>. All judgment being committed to him, we cannot but ask <hi type="italic">how he manages it.</hi> And here he answers, <hi type="italic">My judgment is just.</hi> All Christ's acts of government, both <hi type="italic">legislative</hi> and <hi type="italic">judicial,</hi> are exactly agreeable to the rules of equity; see <reference osisRef="Prov.8.8">Prov. viii. 8</reference>. There can lie no exceptions against any of the determinations of the Redeemer; and therefore, as there shall be no repeal of any of his statutes, so there shall be no appeal from any of his sentences. His judgments are certainly just, for they are directed, <div eID="gen27031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27032" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By the Father's <hi type="italic">wisdom: I can of my ownself</hi> do nothing, nothing without the Father, but <hi type="italic">as I hear I judge,</hi> as he had said before (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">v. 19</reference>), The Son <hi type="italic">can do nothing but what he sees the Father do;</hi> so here, nothing but what he hears the Father <hi type="italic">say: As I hear,</hi> 1. From the secret eternal counsels of the Father, <hi type="italic">so I judge.</hi> Would we know what we may depend upon in our dealing with God? <hi type="italic">Hear the word</hi> of Christ. We need not dive into the divine counsels, those <hi type="italic">secret things</hi> which belong not to us, but attend to the revealed dictates of Christ's government and judgment, which will furnish us with an unerring guide; for what Christ has adjudged is an exact copy or counterpart of what the Father has decreed. 2. From the published records of the Old Testament. Christ, in all the execution of his undertaking, had an eye to the scripture, and made it his business to conform to this, and <hi type="italic">fulfil</hi> it: <hi type="italic">As it was written in the volume of the book.</hi> Thus he taught us to do <hi type="italic">nothing of ourselves,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">as we hear</hi> from the word of God, <hi type="italic">so to judge</hi> of things, and act accordingly. <div eID="gen27032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27033" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By the Father's <hi type="italic">will: My judgment is just,</hi> and cannot be otherwise, <hi type="italic">because I seek not my own will,</hi> but <hi type="italic">his who sent me.</hi> Not as if the will of Christ were contrary to the will of the Father, as the flesh is contrary to the spirit in us; but, 1. Christ had, as man, the natural and innocent affections of the human nature, <hi type="italic">sense of pain</hi> and <hi type="italic">pleasure,</hi> an inclination to life, an aversion to death: yet he <hi type="italic">pleased not himself,</hi> did not confer with these, nor consult these, when he was to go on his undertaking, but acquiesced entirely in the will of his Father. 2. What he did as Mediator was not the result of any <hi type="italic">peculiar</hi> or <hi type="italic">particular</hi> purpose and design of his own; what he did <hi type="italic">seek</hi> to do was not for his own mind's sake, but he was therein guided by his Father's will, and the purpose which he had <hi type="italic">purposed to himself.</hi> This our Saviour did upon all occasions <hi type="italic">refer himself to</hi> and govern himself by.
entries.9e75002954ff6a092f7fdc642598f564ba202392: <div eID="gen27033" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Proves His Divine Mission; Infidelity of the Jews Reproved.</title> <div sID="gen27034" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. <hi type="super">32</hi> There is another that beareth witness of me; and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true. 33 Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth. 34 But I receive not testimony from man: but these things I say, that ye might be saved. <hi type="super">35</hi> He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light. <hi type="super">36</hi> But I have greater witness than <hi type="italic">that</hi> of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me. <hi type="super">37</hi> And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape. <hi type="super">38</hi> And ye have not his word abiding in you: for whom he hath sent, him ye believe not. <hi type="super">39</hi> Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. <hi type="super">40</hi> And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life. <hi type="super">41</hi> I receive not honour from men. 42 But I know you, that ye have not the love of God in you. 43 I am come in my Father's name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive. <hi type="super">44</hi> How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> from God only? <hi type="super">45</hi> Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father: there is <hi type="italic">one</hi> that accuseth you, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Moses, in whom ye trust. <hi type="super">46</hi> For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me. <hi type="super">47</hi> But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words? <div eID="gen27034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27035" type="x-p"/> In these verses our Lord Jesus proves and confirms the commission he had produced, and makes it out that he was sent of God to be the Messiah. <div eID="gen27035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27036" type="x-p"/> I. He <hi type="italic">sets aside</hi> his own testimony of himself (<reference osisRef="John.5.31">v. 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If I bear witness of myself,</hi> though it is infallibly true (<reference osisRef="John.8.14">ch. viii. 14</reference>), yet, according to the common rule of judgment among men, you will not admit it as <hi type="italic">legal proof,</hi> nor allow it to be <hi type="italic">given in evidence.</hi>" Now, 1. This reflects reproach upon the sons of men, and their veracity and integrity. Surely we may say deliberately, what David said in haste, <hi type="italic">All men are liars,</hi> else it would never have been such a received maxim that a man's testimony of himself is suspicious, and not to be relied on; it is a sign that self-love is stronger than the love of truth. And yet, 2. It reflects honour on the Son of God, and bespeaks his wonderful condescension, that, though he is the <hi type="italic">faithful witness,</hi> the truth itself, who may challenge to be credited <hi type="italic">upon his honour,</hi> and his own single testimony, yet he is pleased to <hi type="italic">waive his privilege,</hi> and, for the confirmation of our faith, refers himself to his <hi type="italic">vouchers,</hi> that we may have full satisfaction. <div eID="gen27036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27037" type="x-p"/> II. He produces other witnesses that bear testimony to him that he was sent of God. <div eID="gen27037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27038" type="x-p"/> 1. The Father himself bore testimony to him (<reference osisRef="John.5.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is another that beareth witness.</hi> I take this to be meant of God the Father, for Christ mentions <hi type="italic">his</hi> testimony with his own (<reference osisRef="John.8.18">ch. viii. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">I bear witness of myself, and the Father beareth witness of me.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27039" type="x-p"/> (1.) The seal which the Father put to his commission: He <hi type="italic">beareth witness of me,</hi> not only has done so by a voice from heaven, but still does so by the tokens of his presence with me. See who they are to whom God will bear witness. [1.] Those whom he <hi type="italic">sends</hi> and <hi type="italic">employs;</hi> where he gives commissions he give credentials. [2.] Those who <hi type="italic">bear witness</hi> to him; so Christ did. God will own and honour those that own and honour him. [3.] Those who decline <hi type="italic">bearing witness of themselves;</hi> so Christ did. God will take care that those who humble and abase themselves, and seek not their own glory, shall not <hi type="italic">lose by it.</hi> <div eID="gen27039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> (2.) The satisfaction Christ had in this testimony: "<hi type="italic">I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true.</hi> I am very well assured that I have a divine mission, and do not in the least hesitate concerning it; thus he had the <hi type="italic">witness in himself.</hi>" The devil tempted him to question his being the Son of God, but he never yielded. <div eID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27041" type="x-p"/> 2. John Baptist witnessed to Christ, <reference osisRef="John.5.33">v. 33</reference>, &c. John came to <hi type="italic">bear witness of the light</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.7">ch. i. 7</reference>); his business was to prepare his way, and direct people to him: <hi type="italic">Behold the Lamb of God.</hi> <div eID="gen27041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27042" type="x-p"/> (1.) Now the testimony of John was, [1.] A <hi type="italic">solemn</hi> and public testimony: "You sent an embassy of priests and Levites to John, which gave him an opportunity of publishing what he had to say; it was not a popular, but a judicial testimony." [2.] It was a <hi type="italic">true</hi> testimony: <hi type="italic">He bore witness to the truth,</hi> as a witness ought to do, the <hi type="italic">whole truth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">nothing but the truth.</hi> Christ does not say, <hi type="italic">He bore witness to me</hi> (though every one knew he did), but, like an honest man, <hi type="italic">He bore witness to the truth.</hi> Now John was confessedly such a holy, good man, so mortified to the world, and so conversant with divine things, that it could not be imagined he should be guilty of such a forgery and imposture as to say what he did concerning Christ if it had not been so, and if he had not been sure of it. <div eID="gen27042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27043" type="x-p"/> (2.) Two things are added concerning John's testimony:— <div eID="gen27043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27044" type="x-p"/> [1.] That it was a testimony <hi type="italic">ex abundanti</hi>—<hi type="italic">more than he needed to vouch</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">I receive not testimony from man.</hi> Though Christ saw fit to quote John's testimony, it was with a protestation that it shall not be deemed or construed so as to prejudice the prerogative of his self-sufficiency. Christ needs no letters or commendation, no testimonials or certificates, but what his own worth and excellency bring with him; why then did Christ here urge the testimony of John? Why, <hi type="italic">these things I say, that you may be saved.</hi> This he aimed at in all this discourse, to save not his own life, but the souls of others; he produced John's testimony because, being one <hi type="italic">of themselves,</hi> it was to be hoped that they would hearken to it. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ desires and designs the salvation even of his enemies and persecutors. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The word of Christ is the ordinary means of salvation. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Christ in his word considers our infirmities and condescends to our capacities, consulting not so much what it befits so great a prince to say as what we can bear, and what will be most likely to do us good. <div eID="gen27044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27045" type="x-p"/> [2.] That it was a testimony <hi type="italic">ad hominem</hi>—<hi type="italic">to the man,</hi> because John Baptist was one whom <hi type="italic">they</hi> had a respect for (<reference osisRef="John.5.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">He was a light</hi> among you. <div eID="gen27045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27046" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The character of John Baptist: <hi type="italic">He was a burning and a shining light.</hi> Christ often spoke honourably of John; he was now in prison under a cloud, yet Christ gives him his <hi type="italic">due praise,</hi> which we must be ready to do to all that faithfully serve God. 1. He was a <hi type="italic">light,</hi> not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">phos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">lux, light</hi> (so Christ was <hi type="italic">the</hi> light), but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">lyknos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">lucerna, a luminary,</hi> a derived subordinate light. His office was to enlighten a dark world with notices of the Messiah's approach, to whom he was as the <hi type="italic">morning star.</hi> 2. He was a <hi type="italic">burning</hi> light, which denotes <hi type="italic">sincerity;</hi> painted fire may be made to shine, but that which burns is true fire. It denotes also his <hi type="italic">activity,</hi> zeal, and fervency, burning in love to God and the souls of men; fire is always working on itself or something else, so is a good minister. 3. He was a <hi type="italic">shining</hi> light, which denotes either his <hi type="italic">exemplary conversation,</hi> in which our light should shine (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Matt. v. 16</reference>), or an <hi type="italic">eminent</hi> diffusive influence. He was illustrious in the sight of others; though he affected obscurity and retirement, and was <hi type="italic">in the deserts,</hi> yet such were his doctrine, his baptism, his life, that he became very <hi type="italic">remarkable,</hi> and attracted the eyes of the nation. <div eID="gen27046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27047" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The affections of the people to him: <hi type="italic">you were willing for a season to rejoice in his light.</hi> 1. It was a <hi type="italic">transport</hi> that they were <hi type="italic">in,</hi> upon the appearing of John: "<hi type="italic">You were willing</hi>— <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ethelesate</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">you delighted to rejoice in his light;</hi> you were very proud that you had such a man among you, who was the honour of your country; you were willing <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">agalliasthenai</hi></hi>—willing to <hi type="italic">dance,</hi> and make a noise about this light, as boys about a bonfire." 2. It was but <hi type="italic">transient,</hi> and soon over: "You were fond of him, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pros horan</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for an hour,</hi> for <hi type="italic">a season,</hi> as little children are fond of a new thing, you were pleased with John awhile, but soon grew weary of him and his ministry, and said that <hi type="italic">he had a devil,</hi> and now you have him in prison." Note, Many, that seem to be affected and pleased with the gospel at first, afterwards despise and reject it; it is common for forward and noisy professors to cool and fall off. These here rejoiced in John's light, but never walked in it, and therefore did not keep to it; they were like the stony ground. While Herod was a friend to John Baptist, the people caressed him; but when he fell under Herod's frowns he lost their favours: "<hi type="italic">You were willing</hi> to countenance John, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pros horan</hi></hi> that is, for <hi type="italic">temporal ends</hi>" (so some take it); "you were glad of him, in hopes to make a tool of him, by his interest and under the shelter of his name to have shaken off the Roman yoke, and recovered the civil liberty and honour of your country." Now, (1.) Christ mentions their respect to John, to <hi type="italic">condemn</hi> them for their present opposition to himself, to whom John bore witness. If they had continued their veneration for John, as they ought to have done, they would have embraced Christ. (2.) He mentions the passing away of their respect, to justify God in depriving them, as he had now done, of John's ministry, and putting that light under a bushel. <div eID="gen27047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27048" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ's own works witnessed to him (<reference osisRef="John.5.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have a testimony greater than that of John;</hi> for <hi type="italic">if we believe the witness of men</hi> sent of God, as John was, the <hi type="italic">witness of God</hi> immediately, and not by the ministry of men, <hi type="italic">is greater,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.9">1 John v. 9</reference>. Observe, Though the witness of John was a less <hi type="italic">cogent</hi> and less <hi type="italic">considerable</hi> witness, yet our Lord was pleased to make use of it. We must be glad of all the supports that offer themselves for the confirmation of our faith, though they may not amount to a demonstration, and we must not <hi type="italic">invalidate</hi> any, under pretence that there are others more <hi type="italic">conclusive;</hi> we have occasion for them all. Now this greater testimony was that of the <hi type="italic">works</hi> which <hi type="italic">his Father had given him to finish.</hi> That is, (1.) In general the whole course of his life and ministry—his revealing God and his will to us, setting up his kingdom among men, reforming the world, destroying Satan's kingdom, restoring fallen man to his primitive purity and felicity, and shedding abroad in men's hearts the love of God and of one another—all that work of which he said when he died, <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> it was all, from first to last, <hi type="italic">opus Deo dignum—a work worthy of God;</hi> all he said and did was <hi type="italic">holy</hi> and <hi type="italic">heavenly,</hi> and a divine purity, power, and grace shone in it, proving abundantly that he was <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> (2.) In particular. The miracles he wrought for the proof of his divine mission witnessed of him. Now it is here said, [1.] That these works were <hi type="italic">given him by the Father,</hi> that is, he was both <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> and <hi type="italic">empowered</hi> to work them; for, as Mediator, he <hi type="italic">derived</hi> both commission and strength from his Father. [2.] They were given to him to <hi type="italic">finish;</hi> he must do all those works of wonder which the counsel and foreknowledge of God had before determined to be done; and his finishing them proves a divine power; for as <hi type="italic">for God his work is perfect.</hi> [3.] These works did <hi type="italic">bear witness of him,</hi> did prove that he was sent of God, and that what he said concerning himself was true; see <reference osisRef="Heb.2.4">Heb. ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.22">Acts ii. 22</reference>. That the Father had sent him as <hi type="italic">a Father,</hi> not as a master sends his servant on an errand, but as a father sends his son to take possession for himself; if God had not sent him, he would not have <hi type="italic">seconded</hi> him, would not have <hi type="italic">sealed</hi> him, as he did by the works he gave him to do; for the world's Creator will never be its deceiver. <div eID="gen27048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27049" type="x-p"/> 4. He produces, more fully than before, his Father's testimony concerning him (<reference osisRef="John.5.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Father that sent me hath borne witness of me.</hi> The prince is not accustomed to follow his ambassador himself, to confirm his commission <hi type="italic">viva voce—by speaking;</hi> but God was pleased to bear witness of his Son himself by a voice from heaven at his baptism (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>): This is my ambassador, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> The Jews reckoned <hi type="italic">Bath-kol;—the daughter of a voice,</hi> a voice from heaven, one of the ways by which God made known his mind; and in that way he had owned Christ publicly and solemnly, and repeated it, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">Matt. xvii. 5</reference>. Note, (1.) Those whom God <hi type="italic">sends</hi> he will <hi type="italic">bear witness</hi> of; where he gives a commission, he will not fail to seal it; he that never <hi type="italic">left himself without witness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Acts xiv. 17</reference>) will never leave any of his servants so, who go upon his errand. (2.) Where God demands belief, he will not fail to give sufficient <hi type="italic">evidence,</hi> as he has done concerning Christ. That which was to be witnessed concerning Christ was chiefly this, that the God we had offended was willing to accept of him as a Mediator. Now concerning this he has <hi type="italic">himself</hi> given us full satisfaction (and he was fittest to do it), declaring himself well-pleased in him; if we be so, the work is done. Now, it might be suggested, if God himself thus bore witness of Christ, how came it to pass that he was not universally received by the Jewish nation and their rulers? To this Christ here answers that it was not to be thought strange, nor could their infidelity weaken his credibility, for two reasons:—[1.] Because they were not acquainted with such extraordinary revelations of God and his will: <hi type="italic">You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape,</hi> or <hi type="italic">appearance.</hi> They showed themselves to be as ignorant of God, though they professed relation to him, as we are of a man we never either saw or heard. "But why do I talk to you of God's bearing witness of me? He is one you know nothing of, nor have any acquaintance or communion with." Note, Ignorance of God is the true reason of men's rejecting the record he has given concerning his Son. A right understanding of <hi type="italic">natural religion</hi> would discover to us such admirable congruities in the <hi type="italic">Christian</hi> religion as would greatly dispose our minds to the entertainment of it. Some give this sense of it: "The Father bore witness of me by a <hi type="italic">voice,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">descent of a dove,</hi> which is such an extraordinary thing that you never saw or heard the like; and yet for my sake there was such a voice and appearance; yea, and you might have <hi type="italic">heard that voice,</hi> you might have <hi type="italic">seen that appearance,</hi> as others did, if you had closely attended the ministry of John, but by slighting it you missed of that testimony." [2.] Because they were not affected, no, not with the ordinary ways by which God had revealed himself to them: <hi type="italic">You have not his word abiding in you,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.38">v. 38</reference>. They had the scriptures of the Old Testament; might they not by them be disposed to receive Christ? Yes, if they had had their due influence upon them. But, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The word of God was not in them; it was <hi type="italic">among them,</hi> in their country, in their hands, but not <hi type="italic">in them,</hi> in their hearts; not ruling in their souls, but only shining in their eyes and sounding in their ears. What did it avail them that they had the oracles of God <hi type="italic">committed</hi> to them (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.2">Rom. iii. 2</reference>), when they had not these oracles <hi type="italic">commanding</hi> in them? If they had, they would readily have embraced Christ. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It did not <hi type="italic">abide.</hi> Many have the word of God coming into them, and making some impressions for awhile, but it does not <hi type="italic">abide</hi> with them; it is not constantly in them, as a man at home, but only now and then, as a <hi type="italic">wayfaring man.</hi> If the word <hi type="italic">abide in</hi> us, if we converse with it by frequent meditation, consult with it upon every occasion, and conform to it in our conversation, we shall then readily receive the witness of the Father concerning Christ; see <reference osisRef="John.7.17">ch. vii. 17</reference>. But how did it appear that they <hi type="italic">had not the word of God abiding in them?</hi> It appeared by this, <hi type="italic">Whom he hath sent, him ye believe not.</hi> There was so much said in the Old Testament concerning Christ, to direct people when and where to look for him, and so to facilitate the discovery of him, that, if they had duly considered these things, they could not have avoided the conviction of Christ's being sent of God; so that their not believing in Christ was a certain sign that the word of God did not abide in them. Note, The in-dwelling of the word, and Spirit, and grace of God in us, is best tried by its effects, particularly by our <hi type="italic">receiving what he sends,</hi> the commands, the messengers, the providences he sends, especially Christ whom he hath sent. <div eID="gen27049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27050" type="x-p"/> 5. The last witness he calls is the Old Testament, which witnessed of him, and to it he appeals (<reference osisRef="John.5.39">v. 39</reference>, &c.): <hi type="italic">Search the scriptures,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ereunate</hi></hi>. <div eID="gen27050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27051" type="x-p"/> (1.) This may be read, either, [1.] "<hi type="italic">You search the scriptures,</hi> and you do well to do so; you read them daily in your synagogues, you have rabbies, and doctors, and scribes, that make it their business to study them, and criticize upon them." The Jews boasted of the flourishing of scripture-learning in the days of Hillel, who died about twelve years after Christ's birth, and reckoned some of those who were then members of the sanhedrim the <hi type="italic">beauties of their wisdom</hi> and the <hi type="italic">glories of their law;</hi> and Christ owns that they did indeed search the scriptures, but it was in search of their <hi type="italic">own glory: "You search the scriptures,</hi> and therefore, if you were not <hi type="italic">wilfully blind,</hi> you would <hi type="italic">believe in me.</hi>" Note, It is possible for men to be very studious in the letter of the scripture, and yet to be strangers to the power and influence of it. Or, [2.] As we read it: <hi type="italic">Search the scriptures;</hi> and so, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was spoken to <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the nature of an <hi type="italic">appeal:</hi> "You profess to receive and believe the scripture; here I will <hi type="italic">join issue</hi> with you, let this be the judge, provided you will not <hi type="italic">rest in the letter" (hærere in cortice</hi>), "but will <hi type="italic">search</hi> into it." Note, when appeals are made to the scriptures, they must be searched. Search the whole book of scripture <hi type="italic">throughout,</hi> compare one passage with another, and explain one by another. We must likewise search particular passages <hi type="italic">to the bottom,</hi> and see not what they <hi type="italic">seem</hi> to say <hi type="italic">prima facie—at the first appearance,</hi> but what they say <hi type="italic">indeed. Secondly,</hi> It is spoken to <hi type="italic">us</hi> in the nature of an <hi type="italic">advice,</hi> or a command to all Christians to search the scriptures. Note, All those who would <hi type="italic">find Christ</hi> must <hi type="italic">search the scriptures;</hi> not only read them, and hear them, but search them, which denotes, 1. <hi type="italic">Diligence</hi> in seeking, labour, and study, and close application of mind. 2. <hi type="italic">Desire</hi> and <hi type="italic">design</hi> of finding. We must aim at some spiritual benefit and advantage in reading and studying the scripture, and often ask, "What am I now searching for?" We must search as for <hi type="italic">hidden treasures</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.4">Prov. ii. 4</reference>), as those that <hi type="italic">sink</hi> for gold or silver, or that <hi type="italic">dive</hi> for pearl, <reference osisRef="Job.28.1-Job.28.11">Job xxviii. 1-11</reference>. This ennobled the Bereans, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Acts xvii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen27051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27052" type="x-p"/> (2.) Now there are two things which we are here directed to have in our eye, in our searching the scripture: <hi type="italic">heaven</hi> our end, and <hi type="italic">Christ</hi> our way. [1.] We must search the scriptures for <hi type="italic">heaven</hi> as our <hi type="italic">great end: For in them you think you have eternal life.</hi> The scripture assures us of an eternal state set before us, and offers to us an eternal life in that state: it contains the <hi type="italic">chart</hi> that <hi type="italic">describes</hi> it, the <hi type="italic">charter</hi> that <hi type="italic">conveys</hi> it, the <hi type="italic">direction</hi> in the way that leads to it, and the <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> upon which the hope of it is built; and this is worth searching for where we are sure to find it. But to the Jews Christ saith only, <hi type="italic">You think</hi> you have <hi type="italic">eternal life</hi> in the scriptures, because, though they did retain the belief and hope of eternal life, and grounded their expectations of it upon the scriptures, yet herein they missed it, that they looked for it by the bare reading and studying of the scripture. It was a common but corrupt saying among them, <hi type="italic">He that has the words of the law has eternal life;</hi> they thought they were sure of heaven if they could say by <hi type="italic">heart,</hi> or rather by <hi type="italic">rote,</hi> such and such passages of scripture as they were directed to by the tradition of the elders; as they thought all the <hi type="italic">vulgar</hi> cursed because they did not thus know the law (<reference osisRef="John.7.49">ch. vii. 49</reference>), so they concluded all the <hi type="italic">learned</hi> undoubtedly <hi type="italic">blessed.</hi> [2.] We must <hi type="italic">search the scriptures</hi> for <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> as the new and living <hi type="italic">way</hi> that leads to this <hi type="italic">end.</hi> These are <hi type="italic">they,</hi> the great and principal witnesses, <hi type="italic">that testify of me.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The scriptures, even those of the Old Testament, <hi type="italic">testify</hi> of Christ, and by them God <hi type="italic">bears witness</hi> to him. The Spirit of Christ in the prophets testified beforehand of him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>), the purposes and promises of God concerning him, and the previous notices of him. The Jews knew very well that the Old Testament testified of the Messiah, and were critical in their remarks upon the passages that looked that way; and yet were careless, and wretchedly overseen, in the application of them. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Therefore</hi> we must <hi type="italic">search the scriptures,</hi> and may hope to find eternal life in that search, because they testify of Christ; for this is <hi type="italic">life eternal, to know him;</hi> see <reference osisRef="1John.5.11">1 John v. 11</reference>. Christ is the treasure hid in the field of the scriptures, the water in those wells, the milk in those breasts. <div eID="gen27052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27053" type="x-p"/> (3.) To this testimony he annexes a reproof of their infidelity and wickedness in four instances; particularly, <div eID="gen27053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27054" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their <hi type="italic">neglect of him</hi> and his doctrine: "<hi type="italic">You will not come tome, that you might have life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.40">v. 40</reference>. You search the scriptures, you believe the prophets, who you cannot but see testify of me; and yet you will not <hi type="italic">come to me,</hi> to whom they direct you." Their estrangement from Christ was the fault not so much of their <hi type="italic">understandings</hi> as of their <hi type="italic">wills.</hi> This is expressed as a complaint; Christ offered life, and it was not accepted. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There is <hi type="italic">life</hi> to be had with Jesus Christ for poor souls; we may have life, the life of <hi type="italic">pardon</hi> and <hi type="italic">grace,</hi> and <hi type="italic">comfort</hi> and <hi type="italic">glory:</hi> life is the perfection of our being, and inclusive of all happiness; and Christ is our life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that would have this life must <hi type="italic">come</hi> to Jesus Christ for it; we may have it for the coming for. It <hi type="italic">supposes</hi> an assent of the understanding to the doctrine of Christ and the record given concerning him; it <hi type="italic">lies in</hi> the consent of the will to his government and grace, and it <hi type="italic">produces</hi> an answerable compliance in the affections and actions. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The only reason why sinners die is because they <hi type="italic">will not come</hi> to Christ for life and happiness; it is not because they <hi type="italic">cannot,</hi> but because they <hi type="italic">will not.</hi> They will neither <hi type="italic">accept</hi> the life offered, because <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> and <hi type="italic">divine,</hi> nor will they <hi type="italic">agree</hi> to the terms on which it is offered, nor <hi type="italic">apply</hi> themselves to the use of the appointed means: they will not be cured, for they will not observe the methods of cure. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The wilfulness and obstinacy of sinners in rejecting the tenders of grace are a great grief to the Lord Jesus, and what he complains of. Those words (<reference osisRef="John.5.41">v. 41</reference>), <hi type="italic">I receive not honour from men,</hi> come in a parenthesis, to obviate an objection against him, as if he sought his own glory, and made himself the head of a party, in obliging all to come to <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and applaud him. Note, 1. He did not <hi type="italic">covet</hi> nor <hi type="italic">court</hi> the applause of men, did not in the least affect that worldly pomp and splendour in which the carnal Jews expected their Messiah to appear. He charged those whom he cured not to make him known, and withdrew from those that would have made him king. 2. He <hi type="italic">had not</hi> the applause of men. Instead of <hi type="italic">receiving honour</hi> from men, he received a great deal of <hi type="italic">dishonour</hi> and disgrace from men, for he made himself of no reputation. 3. He <hi type="italic">needed</hi> not the applause of men; it was no addition to his glory whom all the angels of God worship, nor was he any otherwise pleased with it than as it was according to his Father's will, and for the happiness of those who, in giving honour <hi type="italic">to him,</hi> received much greater honour <hi type="italic">from him.</hi> <div eID="gen27054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27055" type="x-p"/> [2.] Their <hi type="italic">want of the love of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.42">v. 42</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I know you</hi> very well, <hi type="italic">that you have not the love of God in you.</hi> Why should I wonder that you do not come to me, when you want even the first principle of <hi type="italic">natural religion,</hi> which is the <hi type="italic">love of God?</hi>" Note, The reason why people <hi type="italic">slight Christ</hi> is because they do not <hi type="italic">love God;</hi> for, if we did indeed love God, we should love him who is his express image, and hasten to him by whom only we may be restored to the favour of God. He charged them (<reference osisRef="John.5.37">v. 37</reference>) with <hi type="italic">ignorance</hi> of God, and here with want of love to him; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> men have not the love of God because they desire not the knowledge of him. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The crime charged upon them: <hi type="italic">You have not the love of God in you.</hi> They pretended a great love to God, and thought they proved it by their zeal for the law, the temple, and the sabbath; and yet they were really without the love of God. Note, There are many who make a great profession of religion who yet show they want the love of God by their neglect of Christ and their contempt of his commandments; they hate his holiness and undervalue his goodness. Observe, It is the love of God <hi type="italic">in</hi> us, that love seated <hi type="italic">in the heart,</hi> a living active principle there, that God will <hi type="italic">accept;</hi> the love <hi type="italic">shed abroad</hi> there, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Rom. v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The proof of this charge, by the personal knowledge of Christ, who <hi type="italic">searches the heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Rev. ii. 23</reference>) and knows what is <hi type="italic">in man: I know you.</hi> Christ sees through all our disguises, and can say to each of us, <hi type="italic">I know thee.</hi> 1. Christ knows men better than <hi type="italic">their neighbours know them.</hi> The people thought that the scribes and Pharisees were very devout and good men, but Christ knew that they had not the love of God in them. 2. Christ knows men better than <hi type="italic">they know themselves.</hi> These Jews had a very good opinion of themselves, but Christ knew how corrupt their inside was, notwithstanding the speciousness of their outside; we may deceive ourselves, but we cannot deceive him. 3. Christ knows men who do not, and will not, know him; he looks <hi type="italic">on</hi> those who industriously look <hi type="italic">off</hi> from him, and calls by their own name, their true name, those who have not known him. <div eID="gen27055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27056" type="x-p"/> [3.] Another crime charged upon them is their readiness to entertain false Christs and false prophets, while they obstinately opposed him who was the true Messias (<reference osisRef="John.5.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am come in my Father's name, and you receive me not. If another shall come in his own name, him you will receive. Be astonished, O heavens, at this</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.12-Jer.2.13">Jer. ii. 12, 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">for my people have committed two evils,</hi> great evils indeed. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They have <hi type="italic">forsaken the fountain of living waters,</hi> for they would not receive Christ, who came in his Father's name, had his commission from his Father, and did all for his glory. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They have <hi type="italic">hewn out broken cisterns,</hi> they hearken to every one that will set up in his own name. They forsake their own mercies, which is bad enough; and it is for <hi type="italic">lying vanities,</hi> which is worse. Observe here, 1. Those are false prophets who come in their own name, who run without being sent, and set up for themselves only. 2. It is just with God to suffer those to be deceived with false prophets who receive not the truth in the love of it. <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10-2Thess.2.11">2 Thess. ii. 10, 11</reference>. The errors of antichrist are the just punishment of those who obey not the doctrine of Christ. They that shut their eyes against the true light are by the judgment of God given up to wander endlessly after <hi type="italic">false lights,</hi> and to be led aside after every <hi type="italic">ignis fatuus.</hi> 3. It is the gross folly of many that, while they <hi type="italic">nauseate</hi> ancient truths, they are <hi type="italic">fond</hi> of upstart errors; they loathe manna, and at the same time <hi type="italic">feed upon ashes.</hi> After the Jews had rejected Christ and his gospel, they were continually haunted with spectres, with <hi type="italic">false Christs</hi> and <hi type="italic">false prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Matt. xxiv. 24</reference>), and their proneness to follow such occasioned those distractions and seditions that hastened their ruin. <div eID="gen27056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27057" type="x-p"/> [4.] They are here charged with pride and vain-glory, and unbelief, the effect of them, <reference osisRef="John.5.44">v. 44</reference>. Having sharply reproved their unbelief, like a wise physician, he here searches into the cause, lays the axe to the root. They <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> slighted and undervalued Christ because they <hi type="italic">admired</hi> and <hi type="italic">overvalued</hi> themselves. Here is, <div eID="gen27057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27058" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their ambition of worldly honour. Christ despised it, <reference osisRef="John.5.41">v. 41</reference>. They set their hearts upon it: <hi type="italic">You receive honour one of another;</hi> that is, "You look for a Messiah in outward pomp, and promise yourselves worldly honour by him." <hi type="italic">You receive honour:</hi>—1. "You desire to receive it, and aim at this in all you do." 2. "You give honour to others, and applaud them, only that they may return it, and may applaud you." <hi type="italic">Petimus dabimusque vicissim—We ask and we bestow.</hi> It is the proud man's art to throw honour upon others only that it may rebound upon himself. 3. "You are very careful to keep all the honours to yourselves, and confine them to your own party, as if you had the monopoly of that which is honourable." 4. "What respect is shown to you you <hi type="italic">receive</hi> yourselves, and do not transmit to God, as Herod." Idolizing men and their sentiments, and affecting to be idolized by them and their applauses, are pieces of idolatry as directly contrary to Christianity as any other. <div eID="gen27058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27059" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their neglect of spiritual honour, called here <hi type="italic">the honour that comes from God only;</hi> this they sought not, nor minded. Note, 1. True honour is that which <hi type="italic">comes from God only,</hi> that is real and lasting honour; those are honourable indeed whom he takes into covenant and communion with himself. 2. <hi type="italic">This honour have all the saints.</hi> All that believe in Christ, through him receive the honour that comes from God. He is not partial, but will give glory wherever he gives grace. 3. This honour that comes from God we must <hi type="italic">seek,</hi> must aim at it, and act for it, and take up with nothing short of it (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>); we must account it <hi type="italic">our reward,</hi> as the Pharisees accounted the praise of men. 4. Those that will not come to Christ, and those that are ambitious of worldly honour, make it appear that they seek not the honour that comes from God, and it is their folly and ruin. <div eID="gen27059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27060" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The influence this had upon their infidelity. <hi type="italic">How can you believe</hi> who are thus affected? Observe here, 1. The difficulty of believing arises from ourselves and our own corruption; we make our work hard to ourselves, and then complain it is impracticable. 2. The ambition and affectation of worldly honour are a great hindrance to faith in Christ. How can they believe who make the praise and applause of men their idol? When the profession and practice of serious godliness are unfashionable, are <hi type="italic">every where spoken against,</hi>—when Christ and his followers are men wondered at, and to be a Christian is to be like a <hi type="italic">speckled bird</hi> (and this is the common case),—how can they believe the summit of whose ambition is to <hi type="italic">make a fair show in the flesh?</hi> <div eID="gen27060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27061" type="x-p"/> 6. The last witness here called is Moses, <reference osisRef="John.5.45">v. 45</reference>, &c. The Jews had a great veneration for Moses, and valued themselves upon their being the <hi type="italic">disciples</hi> of Moses, and pretended to adhere to Moses, in their opposition to Christ; but Christ here shows them, <div eID="gen27061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27062" type="x-p"/> (1.) That Moses was a witness against the unbelieving Jews, <hi type="italic">and accused them to the Father: There is one that accuses you, even Moses.</hi> This may be understood either, [1.] As showing the difference between the law and the gospel. Moses, that is, the law, <hi type="italic">accuses you,</hi> for by the law is the knowledge of sin; it <hi type="italic">condemns</hi> you, it is to those that trust to it a ministration of death and condemnation. But it is not the design of Christ's gospel to <hi type="italic">accuse</hi> us: <hi type="italic">Think not that I will accuse you.</hi> Christ did not come into the world as a <hi type="italic">Momus,</hi> to find fault and pick quarrels with every body, or as a <hi type="italic">spy</hi> upon the actions of men, or a <hi type="italic">promoter,</hi> to fish for crimes; no, he came to be an advocate, not an accuser; to reconcile God and man, and not to set them more at variance. What fools were they then that adhered to Moses against Christ, and <hi type="italic">desired to be under the law!</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.21">Gal. iv. 21</reference>. Or, [2.] As showing the manifest unreasonableness of their infidelity: "Think not that I will appeal from your bar to God's and challenge you to answer there for what you do against me, as injured innocency usually does; no, I do not need; you are already accused, and cast, in the court of heaven; Moses himself says enough to convict you of, and condemn you for, your unbelief." Let them not mistake <hi type="italic">concerning Christ;</hi> though he was a prophet, he did not improve his interest in heaven against those that persecuted him, did not, as Elias, <hi type="italic">make intercession against Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.2">Rom. vi. 2</reference>), nor as Jeremiah desire to <hi type="italic">see God's vengeance on them.</hi> Nor let them mistake concerning Moses, as if he would stand by them in rejecting Christ; no, <hi type="italic">There is one that accuses you, even Moses in whom you trust.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> External privileges and advantages are commonly the vain confidence of those who reject Christ and his grace. The Jews <hi type="italic">trusted</hi> in Moses, and thought their having his laws and ordinances would save them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that confide in their privileges, and do not improve them, will find not only that their confidence is disappointed, but that those very privileges will be witnesses against them. <div eID="gen27062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27063" type="x-p"/> (2.) That Moses was a witness for Christ and to his doctrine (<reference osisRef="John.5.46-John.5.47">v. 46, 47</reference>): <hi type="italic">He wrote of me.</hi> Moses did particularly prophesy of Christ, as the Seed of the woman, the Seed of Abraham, the Shiloh, the great Prophet; the ceremonies of the law of Moses were <hi type="italic">figures of him that was to come.</hi> The Jews made Moses the patron of their opposition to Christ; but Christ here shows them their error, that Moses was so far from writing against Christ that he wrote <hi type="italic">for him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">of him.</hi> But, [1.] Christ here charges it on the Jews that they <hi type="italic">did not believe Moses.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="John.5.45">v. 45</reference>) that they <hi type="italic">trusted</hi> in Moses, and yet here he undertakes to make out that they did not believe Moses; they trusted to his name, but they did not receive his doctrine in its true sense and meaning; they did not rightly understand, nor give credit to, what there was in the writings of Moses concerning the Messiah. [2.] He proves this charge from their disbelief of him: <hi type="italic">Had you believed Moses, you would have believed me.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The surest trial of faith is by the effects it produces. Many say that they believe whose actions give their words the lie; for had they believed the scriptures they would have done otherwise than they did. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those who rightly believe one part of scripture will receive every part. The prophecies of the old Testament were so fully accomplished in Christ that those who rejected Christ did in effect deny those prophecies, and set them aside. [3.] From their disbelief of Moses he infers that it was not strange that they rejected him: <hi type="italic">If you believe not his writings, how shall you believe my words?</hi> How can it be thought that you should? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "If you do not believe sacred <hi type="italic">writings,</hi> those oracles which are in black and white, which is the most certain way of conveyance, <hi type="italic">how shall you believe my words,</hi> words being usually less regarded?" <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "If you do not believe Moses, for whom you have such a profound veneration, how is it likely that you should believe me, whom you look upon with so much contempt?" See <reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">Exod. vi. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> "If you believe not what Moses spoke and wrote of me, which is a strong and cogent testimony for me, how shall you believe me and my mission?" If we admit not the premises, how shall we admit the conclusion? The truth of the Christian religion, it being a matter purely of divine revelation, depends upon the divine authority of the scripture; if therefore we believe not the divine inspiration of those writings, how shall be receive the doctrine of Christ?  <chapter eID="John.5"/> <div eID="gen27063" type="x-p"/>

entries.89ecac457da8f6687c68a4310243ee4c16e1fcc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14960"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.5.1-John.5.47">Joh 5:1-47</reference>. The Impotent Man Healed--Discourse Occasioned by the Persecution Arising Thereupon.</title> <div sID="gen28850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14960"/><hi type="bold">1. a feast of the Jews--</hi>What feast? No question has more divided the Harmonists of the Gospels, and the duration of our Lord's ministry may be said to hinge on it. For if, as the majority have thought (until of late years) it was a Passover, His ministry lasted three and a half years; if not, probably a year less. Those who are dissatisfied with the Passover-view all differ among themselves what other feast it was, and some of the most acute think there are no grounds for deciding. In our judgment the evidence is in favor of its being a Passover, but the reasons cannot be stated here. <div eID="gen28850" type="x-p"/>
entries.80d7ae32da6e2f5d8fd85b07fd4eeee97b275e0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14961"/><div sID="gen28851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14961"/><hi type="bold">2-3. sheep market--</hi>The supplement should be (as in Margin) "sheep [gate]," mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Ne 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.32">32</reference>.<div eID="gen28851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bethesda--</hi>that is, "house (place) of mercy," from the cures wrought there.<div eID="gen28852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">five porches--</hi>for shelter to the patients. <div eID="gen28853" type="x-p"/>
entries.3562bb94b19ebd25920259e632cbef2d30aa71ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14963"/><div sID="gen28855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14963"/><hi type="bold">4. an angel, &c.--</hi>This miracle differed in two points from all other miracles recorded in Scripture: (1) It was not one, but a succession of miracles periodically wrought: (2) As it was only wrought "when the waters were troubled," so only upon one patient at a time, and that the patient "who first stepped in after the troubling of the waters." But this only the more undeniably fixed its miraculous character. We have heard of many waters having a medicinal virtue; but what water was ever known to cure instantaneously a single disease? And who ever heard of any water curing all, even the most diverse diseases--"blind, halt, withered"--alike? Above all, who ever heard of such a thing being done "only at a certain season," and most singularly of all, doing it only to the first person who stepped in after the moving of the waters? Any of these peculiarities--much more all taken together--must have proclaimed the supernatural character of the cures wrought. (If the text here be genuine, there can be no doubt of the miracle, as there were multitudes living when this Gospel was published who, from their own knowledge of Jerusalem, could have exposed the falsehood of the Evangelist, if no such cure had been known there. The want of <reference osisRef="John.5.4">Joh 5:4</reference> <hi type="bold">and part of <reference osisRef="John.5.3">Joh 5:3</reference> in some good manuscripts, and the use of some unusual words in the passage, are more easily accounted for than the evidence in their favor if they were not originally in the text. Indeed <reference osisRef="John.5.7">Joh 5:7</reference> is unintelligible without <reference osisRef="John.5.4">Joh 5:4</reference>. The internal evidence brought against it is merely the unlikelihood of such a miracle--</hi>a principle which will carry us a great deal farther if we allow it to weigh against positive evidence). <div eID="gen28855" type="x-p"/>
entries.dba90d80f39322dee68d0af6cfc1a12ff5f9b919: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14964"/><div sID="gen28856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14964"/><hi type="bold">5-9. thirty and eight years--</hi>but not all that time at the pool. This was probably the most pitiable of all the cases, and therefore selected. <div eID="gen28856" type="x-p"/>
entries.a06cd80ba02230f31591d07c79e19df76e099ed1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14969"/><div sID="gen28863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14969"/><hi type="bold">10-16. The Jews--</hi>that is, those in authority. (See on <reference osisRef="John.1.19">Joh 1:19</reference>.)<div eID="gen28863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is not lawful to carry thy bed--</hi>a glorious testimony to the cure, as instantaneous and complete, from the lips of the most prejudiced! (And what a contrast does it, as all our Lord's miracles, present to the bungling miracles of the Church of Rome!) In ordinary circumstances, the rulers had the law on their side (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.15">Ne 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.21">Jr 17:21</reference>). But when the man referred them to "Him that had made him whole" (<reference osisRef="John.5.11">Joh 5:11</reference>) as his authority, the argument was resistless. Yet they ingeniously parried the thrust, asking him, not who had "made him whole"--that would have condemned themselves and defeated their purpose--but who had bidden him "take up his bed and walk," in other words, who had dared to order a breach of the sabbath? It is time we were looking after Him--thus hoping to shake the man's faith in his Healer. <div eID="gen28864" type="x-p"/>
entries.e519d1021238370acd2e272383ed8e9405f19e5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14974"/><div sID="gen28871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14974"/><hi type="bold">17-18. My Father worketh hitherto and I work--</hi>The "I" is emphatic; "The creative and conservative activity of My Father has known no sabbath-cessation from the beginning until now, and that is the law of My working." <div eID="gen28871" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd872daabcfad90ba56b1a5f8c696217760b3072: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14976"/><div sID="gen28874" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14976"/><hi type="bold">19-20. the Son can do nothing of himself--</hi>that is, apart from and in rivalry of the Father, as they supposed. The meaning is, "The Son can have no separate interest or action from the Father."<div eID="gen28874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for what things, &c.--</hi>On the contrary, "whatever the Father doeth that same doeth the Son,"<div eID="gen28875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">likewise--</hi>"in the like manner." What claim to absolute equality with the Father could exceed this: not only to do "the same things," but to do them as the Father does them? <div eID="gen28876" type="x-p"/>
entries.8dc312482555a1e5701b0e58938aa13342989aa0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14978"/><div sID="gen28879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14978"/><hi type="bold">21-23. raiseth the dead and quickeneth them--</hi>one act in two stages. This is His absolute prerogative as God.<div eID="gen28879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so the Son quickeneth them--</hi>that is, raiseth up and quickeneth.<div eID="gen28880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom he will--</hi>not only doing the same divine act, but doing it as the result of His own will, even as the Father does it. This statement is of immense importance in relation to the miracles of Christ, distinguishing them from similar miracles of prophets and apostles, who as human instruments were employed to perform super-natural actions, while Christ did all as the Father's commissioned Servant indeed, but in the exercise of His own absolute right of action. <div eID="gen28881" type="x-p"/>
entries.0412ae0bc7912af81a7f19c2479c04ef276ddaf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14981"/><div sID="gen28886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14981"/><hi type="bold">24. believeth on him that sent me--</hi>that is, believeth in Him as having sent Me. I have spoken of the Son's right not only to heal the sick but to raise from the dead, and quicken whom He will: And now I say unto you, That life-giving operation has already passed upon all who receive My words as the Sent of the Father on the great errand of mercy.<div eID="gen28886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath everlasting life--</hi>immediately on his believing (compare <reference osisRef="John.3.18">Joh 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.12">1Jo 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen28887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is passed--</hi>"hath passed over"<div eID="gen28888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from death unto life--</hi>What a transition! (Compare <reference osisRef="1John.3.14">1Jo 3:14</reference>). <div eID="gen28889" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccd018c429b1076e0d3fe886225e14406307b7ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14982"/><div sID="gen28890" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14982"/><hi type="bold">25-29. The hour cometh--</hi>in its whole fulness, at Pentecost.<div eID="gen28890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and now is--</hi>in its beginnings.<div eID="gen28891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the dead--</hi>the spiritually dead, as is clear from <reference osisRef="John.5.28">Joh 5:28</reference>. Here He rises from the calmer phrase "hearing his word" (<reference osisRef="John.5.24">Joh 5:24</reference>), to the grander expression, "hearing the voice of the Son of God," to signify that as it finds men in a dead condition, so it carries with it a resurrection-power.<div eID="gen28892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall live--</hi>in the sense of <reference osisRef="John.5.24">Joh 5:24</reference>. <div eID="gen28893" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cafdcc3665c960fd94c809b19b5fa073aa26e53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14987"/><div sID="gen28900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14987"/><hi type="bold">30-32. of mine own self do nothing--</hi>that is, apart from the Father, or in any interest than My own. (See on <reference osisRef="John.5.19">Joh 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen28900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as I hear--</hi>that is, "My judgments are all anticipated in the bosom of My Father, to which I have immediate access, and by Me only responded to and reflected. They cannot therefore err, as I live for one end only, to carry into effect the will of Him that sent Me." <div eID="gen28901" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe8051c9a2f9b0dc7717617218ca0fe7229437bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14990"/><div sID="gen28905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14990"/><hi type="bold">33-35. Ye sent unto John--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="John.1.19">Joh 1:19</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen28905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receive not testimony ... from man--</hi>that is, depend not on human testimony.<div eID="gen28906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but ... that ye might be saved--</hi>"I refer to him merely to aid your salvation." <div eID="gen28907" type="x-p"/>
entries.07febbdfaebb759eeacdcd49e2889877052bf624: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14992"/><div sID="gen28911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14992"/><hi type="bold">36-38. I have greater witness--</hi>rather, "The witness which I have is greater."<div eID="gen28911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the works ... bear witness of me--</hi>not simply as miracles nor even as a miracle of mercy, but these miracles, as He did them, with a will and a power, a majesty and a grace manifestly His own. <div eID="gen28912" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb8b0ff1921ab1e7d951ba814a2c4cb64cfa5862: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14995"/><div sID="gen28916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14995"/><hi type="bold">39-42. Search the scriptures, &c.--</hi>"In the Scriptures ye find your charter of eternal life; go search them then, and you will find that I <hi type="bold">am the Great Burden of their testimony; yet ye will not come to Me for that life eternal which you profess to find there, and of which they tell you I am the appointed Dispenser." (Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.12">12</reference>). How touching and gracious are these last words! Observe here (1) The honor which Christ gives to the Scriptures, as a record which all have a right and are bound to search--</hi>the reverse of which the Church of Rome teaches; (2) The opposite extreme is, resting in the mere Book without the living Christ, to direct the soul to whom is its main use and chiefest glory. <div eID="gen28916" type="x-p"/>
entries.4183230b5ec480054cc1741097a6be5667409915: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14998"/><div sID="gen28919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14998"/><hi type="bold">43-47. if another shall come, &c.--</hi>How strikingly has this been verified in the history of the Jews! "From the time of the true Christ to our time, sixty-four false Christs have been reckoned by whom they have been deceived" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen28919" type="x-p"/>

entries.5517e76aa31fed3f03e17cdd32e9f7999d573532: <div eID="gen41737" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen41738" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41739" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41739" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41738" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41740" type="x-p"/> The man who had been diseased thirty-eight years healed on the Sabbath day, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.1-Joh.5.9">Joh 5:1-9</reference>. The Jews cavil, persecute Christ, and seek to kill him, because he had done this cure on the Sabbath, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.10-Joh.5.16">Joh 5:10-16</reference>. Our Lord vindicates his conduct, and shows, from the testimony of the Father, the Scriptures, John the Baptist, and his own works, that he came from God, to be the light and salvation of the world, vv. 17-39. He reproves the Jews for their obstinacy, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.40">Joh 5:40</reference>; hatred to God, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.41">Joh 5:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.42">Joh 5:42</reference>; pride, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.43">Joh 5:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>; and disbelief of their own law, <reference osisRef="Joh.5.45-Joh.5.47">Joh 5:45-47</reference>. <div eID="gen41740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41741" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen41741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41742" type="x-p"/> A feast - This is generally supposed, by the best critics, to have been the feast of the passover, which was the most eminent feast among the Jews. In several excellent MSS. the article is added, ἡ ἑορτη, The feast, the grand, the principal festival. Petavius supposes that the feast of Purim, or lots, is here meant; and one MS. reads ἡ σκηνοπηγια, the feast of Tabernacles. Several of the primitive fathers believe Pentecost to be intended; and they are followed by many of the moderns, because, in <reference osisRef="Joh.7.2">Joh 7:2</reference>, mention is made of the feast of Tabernacles, which followed Pentecost, and was about the latter end of our September; and, in <reference osisRef="Joh.10.22">Joh 10:22</reference>, mention is made of the feast of Dedication, which was held about the latter end of November. See Bp. Pearce. See <reference osisRef="Joh.10.22">Joh 10:22</reference>. <div eID="gen41742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41743" type="x-p"/> Calmet, however, argues that there is no other feast with which all the circumstances marked here so well agree as with the passover; and Bp. Newcome, who is of Calmet's opinion, thinks Bp. Pearce's argument concerning the succession of the feasts to be inconclusive; because it is assumed, not proved, that the three feasts which he mentions above must have happened in the same year. See much on the same subject in Bp. Newcome's notes to his Harmony, p. 15, etc. <div eID="gen41743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41744" type="x-p"/> Lightfoot has observed, that the other evangelists speak very sparingly of our Lord's acts in Judea. They mention nothing of the passovers, from our Lord's baptism till his death, excepting the very last: but John points at them all.
